concepts.title: Computing locally definable construction sequences
concepts.description:
Let r ≥ 1 be an integer, ε > 0 a rational, and 𝒞 a monadically
dependent graph class. There is a constant δ ≥ 1 depending only on 𝒞
such that every n-vertex graph G ∈ 𝒞 has a construction sequence of G
which is radius-r definable with O(r/ε) unary predicates,
O_{𝒞,r,ε}(n^{δε}) parameters and quantifier rank 7, and has length
O_{𝒞,r,ε}(n^{1+δε}). Moreover, there is an algorithm (independent of 𝒞)
which, given r, ε and G, computes such a sequence, and runs in time
Ô_{𝒞,r,ε}(n³) whenever G ∈ 𝒞. Here Ô_k(n³) stands for a bound
O_{k,η}(n^{3+η}) for every η > 0.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The construction sequence is produced by a function `script` of r, ε
and the graph, as a script of `Lax185574.ConstructionSequences`, and
the algorithm `A` computes this function, in the sense of
`Lax185574.Algorithms`. The algorithm, the function and the absolute
constant `K` of the bound O(r/ε) on the number of predicates come first,
so none of them depends on the class. On every graph, the script gives
a construction sequence of the graph. The input of the algorithm is the
triple (r, ε, G), with the encodings of `Lax185574.Encodings`.

The constant δ of the paper is `a`. It is chosen after the class and
before r and ε. The time bound Ô_{𝒞,r,ε}(n³) is spelled out as
`n^(3+η)` for every real η > 0, with the constant `c` depending on 𝒞,
r, ε and η. The same `c` bounds the sequence. The bounds on the
sequence do not involve η, so a single η, say η = 1, gives a constant
for them. The number of unary predicates is at most `⌈K · r/ε⌉ + K`,
which is O(r/ε) in the sense of the paper, including its additive
constant.

Every graph belongs to some monadically dependent class, for instance
the class containing it alone. So the algorithm computes the script of
every graph, at every word length admissible for the constant of some
class that contains it.

Every number in the encoding of the script is at most the length of the
encoding plus n (`Script.HasSmallNumbers`). The paper does not say
this. The algorithm can ensure it by giving the vertices of the initial
partial graph the colors 0, …, n − 1, since steps only use colors that
occur.

namespace Lax185574.DefinableSequences

open Lax185574.Graphs Lax185574.MonadicDependence Lax185574.Algorithms
open Lax185574.ConstructionSequences Lax185574.LocalDefinability

/-- **Locally definable construction sequences.** One algorithm
computes, from `r ≥ 1`, a rational `ε > 0` and a graph `G`, a
construction sequence of `G`, given by its script. On members of a
monadically dependent class it takes time `O(n^(3+η))` for every
`η > 0`, and the sequence has length at most `c · (n+1)^(1+aε)` and is
radius-`r` definable with `⌈K·r/ε⌉ + K` unary predicates,
`⌊c · (n+1)^(aε)⌋` parameters and quantifier rank `7`. Here `a ≥ 1`
depends only on the class, and `c` on the class, `r`, `ε` and `η`. -/
axiom exists_program_definableSequence :
    ∃ (A : Algorithm) (K : ℕ) (script : ℕ → ℚ → (G : Graph) → Script G.n),
      (∀ (r : ℕ) (ε : ℚ) (G : Graph), 1 ≤ r → 0 < ε →
        IsConstructionSequence G.toSimpleGraph (script r ε G).run ∧
          (script r ε G).HasSmallNumbers) ∧
      ∀ C : GraphClass, MonadicallyDependent C → ∃ a : ℕ, 1 ≤ a ∧
        ∀ (r : ℕ) (ε : ℚ), 1 ≤ r → 0 < ε → ∀ η : ℝ, 0 < η → ∃ c : ℕ,
          ∀ G ∈ C,
            A.Computes c (r, ε, G) (script r ε G) ((G.n : ℝ) ^ (3 + η)) ∧

**Locally definable construction sequences.** One algorithm
computes, from `r ≥ 1`, a rational `ε > 0` and a graph `G`, a
construction sequence of `G`, given by its script. On members of a
monadically dependent class it takes time `O(n^(3+η))` for every
`η > 0`, and the sequence has length at most `c · (n+1)^(1+aε)` and is
radius-`r` definable with `⌈K·r/ε⌉ + K` unary predicates,
`⌊c · (n+1)^(aε)⌋` parameters and quantifier rank `7`. Here `a ≥ 1`
depends only on the class, and `c` on the class, `r`, `ε` and `η`.

concepts.title: Local definability bounds the width
concepts.description:
Let q ∈ ℕ and h ≔ 7^q. The following holds for every monadically
dependent graph class 𝒞 and all r, c, s, q₀ ∈ ℕ. If a
construction sequence of a graph G ∈ 𝒞 is radius-(r+h) definable with c
unary predicates, s parameters and rank q₀, then its radius-r depth-q
width is at most O_{𝒞,q,q₀,c}(1) · poly_{𝒞,q,q₀}(s).

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The bound is spelled out as `F · (s + 1)^a`. The exponent `a` depends on
the class, `q` and `q₀`, and the factor `F` additionally on `c`. Neither
depends on `r` or `s`. The paper says that there is a radius increase
h depending on q alone. Its proof takes h = 7^q, the radius of
`Lax185574.LocalToGlobal`, and the statement here names this value,
because the algorithm of `Lax185574.FewTypes` computes the radius from
q.

/-- **Local definability bounds the width.** A construction sequence of
a member of a monadically dependent class that is radius-`(r + 7^q)`
definable with `c` unary predicates, `s` parameters and rank `q₀` has
radius-`r` depth-`q` width at most `F · (s + 1)^a`. -/
axiom width_le_of_isRadiusDefinable (q : ℕ) (C : GraphClass) (hC : MonadicallyDependent C)
    (q₀ : ℕ) :
    ∃ a : ℕ, ∀ c : ℕ, ∃ F : ℕ, ∀ r s : ℕ, ∀ G ∈ C,

        IsRadiusDefinable G.toSimpleGraph seq (r + 7 ^ q) c s q₀ →
          width r q seq ≤ F * (s + 1) ^ a

end Lax185574.DefinableToTypes

concepts.title: Distance logic over partial graphs and distance rank
concepts.description:
The logic distFO extends first-order logic over partial graphs by
*distance atoms*. Its atoms are

- the first-order atoms x = y, E(x, y), N(x, y) and Y(x), for colors Y;
- for each radius r ∈ ℕ, the *binary distance atom* dist(x, y) ≤ r;
- for each radius r ∈ ℕ and color Y, the *unary distance atom*
  dist(x, Y) < r, equivalent to ∃y (Y(y) ∧ dist(x, y) < r).

Distances are measured in the Gaifman graph of the partial graph, that
is, along resolved pairs. A formula is built from atoms by negation,
conjunction and the *local quantifier* ∃y (dist(xᵢ, y) ≤ s ∧ φ(x̄ y)).

The horizon functions are ρ⁻(k, q) = 9^((k+q+1)q) and
ρ⁺(k, q) = 9^((k+q)(q+1)). A formula has *distance rank (k, q)* if it is
a Boolean combination of

- first-order atoms,
- binary distance atoms of radius at most ρ⁻(k, q),
- unary distance atoms of radius at most ρ⁺(k, q), and
- formulas ∃y (dist(xᵢ, y) ≤ ρ⁺(k+1, q−1) ∧ φ(x̄ y)), where q ≥ 1, xᵢ is a
  free variable and φ has distance rank (k+1, q−1).

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
As in `Lax3.FirstOrder`, free variables are counted: `DistFO ℓ` has ℓ
free variables `Fin ℓ`, and the local quantifier binds the new last
variable. The radius of a local quantifier is part of the syntax, and
the distance rank requires it to be exactly ρ⁺(k+1, q−1), as in the
paper. The horizon functions are those of `Lax3.DistFO`, which are the
functions of the paper.

"dist(x, y) ≤ r" holds if a walk of length at most r joins the two
vertices along resolved pairs. "dist(x, Y) < r" holds if some vertex of
color Y is joined to x by a walk of length less than r. In particular
it is false for r = 0.

The works that the paper cites for this logic also allow the
unrestricted quantifier ∃y φ(x̄ y), and call the formulas of distance
rank (k, q) *local*. The paper considers only these formulas, and omits
the adjective. So the syntax here has the local quantifier only, and the
formulas of distance rank (k, q) are the same as in the paper.

Formulas are handed to algorithms in the derived encoding of
`Lax185574.Encoding`, a prefix code: the number of the constructor,
from 0 for `eq` to 8 for `exLocal`, followed by the arguments in order.

namespace Lax185574.DistanceLogic

open Lax185574.PartialGraphs Lax185574.GaifmanGraph Lax185574.Encoding
open Lax3.DistFO (rhoMinus rhoPlus)

/-- Formulas of distance logic over partial graphs with `ℓ` free
variables. -/
inductive DistFO : ℕ → Type
  /-- `xᵢ = xⱼ`. -/
  | eq {ℓ : ℕ} (i j : Fin ℓ) : DistFO ℓ
  /-- `E(xᵢ, xⱼ)`. -/
  | edge {ℓ : ℕ} (i j : Fin ℓ) : DistFO ℓ
  /-- `N(xᵢ, xⱼ)`. -/
  | nonEdge {ℓ : ℕ} (i j : Fin ℓ) : DistFO ℓ
  /-- `Y(xᵢ)`. -/
  | color {ℓ : ℕ} (Y : ℕ) (i : Fin ℓ) : DistFO ℓ
  /-- `dist(xᵢ, xⱼ) ≤ r`. -/
  | distLe {ℓ : ℕ} (r : ℕ) (i j : Fin ℓ) : DistFO ℓ
  /-- `dist(xᵢ, Y) < r`. -/
  | distColorLt {ℓ : ℕ} (r Y : ℕ) (i : Fin ℓ) : DistFO ℓ
  /-- Negation. -/
  | not {ℓ : ℕ} (φ : DistFO ℓ) : DistFO ℓ
  /-- Conjunction. -/
  | and {ℓ : ℕ} (φ ψ : DistFO ℓ) : DistFO ℓ
  /-- `∃y (dist(xᵢ, y) ≤ s ∧ φ(x̄ y))`, binding the new last variable. -/
  | exLocal {ℓ : ℕ} (i : Fin ℓ) (s : ℕ) (φ : DistFO (ℓ + 1)) : DistFO ℓ
  deriving Encode

namespace DistFO

/-- The formula is an atom. -/
def IsAtom {ℓ : ℕ} : DistFO ℓ → Prop
  | .not _ | .and _ _ | .exLocal _ _ _ => False
  | _ => True

/-- Some walk of length less than `r` joins `u` and `v`. -/
def WithinDistLt {W : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph W) (r : ℕ) (u v : W) : Prop :=
  ∃ p : G.Walk u v, p.length < r

variable {V : Type*}

/-- Satisfaction in the partial graph `G` under the assignment `m` of
vertices to the free variables. -/
def Sat (G : PartialGraph V) : {ℓ : ℕ} → (Fin ℓ → V) → DistFO ℓ → Prop
  | _, m, .eq i j => m i = m j
  | _, m, .edge i j => G.edge.Adj (m i) (m j)
  | _, m, .nonEdge i j => G.nonEdge.Adj (m i) (m j)
  | _, m, .color Y i => G.color (m i) = Y
  | _, m, .distLe r i j => WithinDist G.resolved r (m i) (m j)
  | _, m, .distColorLt r Y i => ∃ v, G.color v = Y ∧ WithinDistLt G.resolved r (m i) v
  | _, m, .not φ => ¬ Sat G m φ
  | _, m, .and φ ψ => Sat G m φ ∧ Sat G m ψ
  | _, m, .exLocal i s φ =>
      ∃ v, WithinDist G.resolved s (m i) v ∧ Sat G (Fin.snoc m v) φ

/-- `DRank k q φ`: the formula `φ` has distance rank `(k, q)`. -/
inductive DRank : ℕ → ℕ → {ℓ : ℕ} → DistFO ℓ → Prop
  | eq {k q ℓ : ℕ} (i j : Fin ℓ) : DRank k q (.eq i j)
  | edge {k q ℓ : ℕ} (i j : Fin ℓ) : DRank k q (.edge i j)
  | nonEdge {k q ℓ : ℕ} (i j : Fin ℓ) : DRank k q (.nonEdge i j)
  | color {k q ℓ : ℕ} (Y : ℕ) (i : Fin ℓ) : DRank k q (.color Y i)
  | distLe {k q ℓ : ℕ} (r : ℕ) (i j : Fin ℓ) :
      r ≤ rhoMinus k q → DRank k q (.distLe r i j)
  | distColorLt {k q ℓ : ℕ} (r Y : ℕ) (i : Fin ℓ) :
      r ≤ rhoPlus k q → DRank k q (.distColorLt r Y i)
  | not {k q ℓ : ℕ} {φ : DistFO ℓ} : DRank k q φ → DRank k q (.not φ)
  | and {k q ℓ : ℕ} {φ ψ : DistFO ℓ} :
      DRank k q φ → DRank k q ψ → DRank k q (.and φ ψ)
  | exLocal {k q ℓ : ℕ} (i : Fin ℓ) {φ : DistFO (ℓ + 1)} :
      DRank (k + 1) q φ → DRank k (q + 1) (.exLocal i (rhoPlus (k + 1) q) φ)

end DistFO

end Lax185574.DistanceLogic

concepts.title: The distance matrix of a partial graph
concepts.description:
The *distance matrix* of a partial graph G is the |G| × |G| matrix D_G
with entries D_G(u, v) = dist^G(u, v) ∈ ℕ ∪ {∞}.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The distance is the extended distance `SimpleGraph.edist` of mathlib in
the graph of resolved pairs, a value in `ℕ∞`. So D_G is 0 on the
diagonal, and ∞ for vertices in different components of the graph of
resolved pairs. The matrix of a partial graph on `Fin n` is a function
of two vertices.

Algorithms receive the matrix in the encoding of `Lax185574.Encodings`.
A distance in ℕ ∪ {∞} is encoded as one entry, 0 for ∞ and d + 1 for a
finite distance d. The matrix is the family of its rows, and each row is
the family of its entries. So the word of D_G is n, followed by every
row in order as n and the n entries of the row. Every row has n + 1
entries, the word has length 1 + n(n + 1), and the entry at (u, v) is at
position 2 + u(n + 1) + v, counting from 0. The paper does not say how
∞ is represented. Its bounds O(|G|²) for reading the matrix need entries
of constant size, which this encoding provides.

concepts.title: Encoding data as lists of numbers
concepts.description:
A random access machine reads its input as a list of natural numbers and
writes its output as one. An object is handed to an algorithm through an
*encoding*, a map from its type to lists of numbers. The encodings in
this submission follow one rule, with a few exceptions.

* A natural number is the one-element list containing it.
* A value of an inductive type is a constructor applied to some
  arguments. Its encoding is the number of the constructor (counting
  from 0 in the order of declaration), followed by the encodings of the
  arguments in order. If the type has only one constructor, the number is
  left out.

Arguments that are proofs carry no information and are left out. So are
the implicit arguments that the type of the value determines, such as
the number of free variables of a formula.

For example, the pair `(3, true)` is encoded as `3, 1`, since `true` is
the second constructor of `Bool`. An element `i` of `Fin n` is a natural
number together with a proof that it is less than `n`, so it is encoded
as `i`.

The exceptions are listed in `Lax185574.Encodings`. The main ones are
lists and finite sets. A list is encoded by its length, followed by the
encodings of its entries, so the list `[7, 8]` is encoded as `2, 7, 8`.
A finite set is encoded by the list of the encodings of its elements, in
increasing order.

Each such encoding is a prefix code. An algorithm that knows the type
can read the encoding from the front, one constructor or one length at a
time, without knowing where it ends. The encoding has length linear in
the size of the value, and every number in it is a number of the value,
the number of a constructor or the length of a list. Some of the other
exceptions write further numbers, such as d + 1 for a finite value d of
ℕ∞.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The rule is the class `Encode` together with `deriving Encode`, a
deriving handler that writes the encoding function of an inductive type
from its declaration, by structural recursion. The handler is the
counterpart of Lean's own `deriving Hashable`, with the constructor number
and the encodings of the arguments in place of hashes. It supports
recursive types and indexed families. It rejects mutual and nested
inductive types, and it rejects an implicit argument that the type of the
constructor does not determine, since leaving such an argument out could
lose information. Natural numbers are the only base case. They are an
inductive type too, but their derived encoding would be unary, so their
instance is written by hand.

Lists are an inductive type as well. Their derived encoding would mark
every entry with the number of `cons`. The length in front is the usual
convention, and it lets an algorithm skip a list, or find its end,
without reading its entries.

Types whose values are not built from constructors, such as graphs given
by an adjacency relation, are encoded through an explicit representation
by an encodable type, as the graphs of `Lax185574.Encodings`.

The size of a value, in bounds on running times and on outputs, is the
length of its encoding, `wordLength`.

No decoding function is part of the definition. A statement about an
algorithm only fixes what it reads and what it must write, and these are
determined by the encoding alone.

by an adjacency relation, are encoded through an explicit representation
by an encodable type, as the graphs of `Lax185574.Encodings`.

The size of a value, in bounds on running times and on outputs, is the
length of its encoding, `wordLength`.

No decoding function is part of the definition. A statement about an
algorithm only fixes what it reads and what it must write, and these are
determined by the encoding alone.
-/

namespace Lax185574.Encoding

universe u

/-- An encoding of the values of `α` as lists of natural numbers. -/
class Encode (α : Type u) where
  /-- The list of numbers encoding a value. -/
  encode : α → List ℕ

export Encode (encode)

/-- The size `‖a‖` of a value, as used in running-time bounds: the
length of its encoding. -/
def wordLength {α : Type u} [Encode α] (a : α) : ℕ := (encode a).length

/-- A natural number is encoded as itself. -/
instance : Encode ℕ where
  encode n := [n]

section Deriving

open Lean Elab Command Meta Term Deriving
open Lean.Parser.Term

/-- The match expression of the derived encoding function: one
alternative per constructor, whose right-hand side is the constructor
number (if there are several constructors) followed by the encodings of
the explicit arguments that are not proofs. Recursive arguments are
encoded by a recursive call. -/
def mkEncodeMatch (ctx : Deriving.Context) (header : Header) (indVal : InductiveVal) :
    TermElabM Term := do
  let discrs ← mkDiscrs header indVal
  if indVal.ctors.isEmpty then
    return ← `(nomatch $(mkIdent header.targetNames[0]!):ident)
  let mut alts : Array (TSyntax ``matchAlt) := #[]
  for ctorName in indVal.ctors, ctorIdx in [0:indVal.ctors.length] do
    let ctorInfo ← getConstInfoCtor ctorName
    let alt : TSyntax ``matchAlt ← forallTelescopeReducing ctorInfo.type fun xs resultType => do
      let mut patterns : Array Term := #[]
      for _ in [0:indVal.numIndices] do
        patterns := patterns.push (← `(_))
      let mut ctorArgs : Array Term := #[]
      for _ in [0:indVal.numParams] do
        ctorArgs := ctorArgs.push (← `(_))
      let mut parts : Array Term := #[]
      if indVal.ctors.length > 1 then
        parts := parts.push (← `([$(quote ctorIdx)]))
      for i in [0:ctorInfo.numFields] do
        let x := xs[indVal.numParams + i]!
        let a := mkIdent (← mkFreshUserName `a)
        ctorArgs := ctorArgs.push a
        let decl ← x.fvarId!.getDecl
        let xTy ← whnf decl.type
        if ← isProp decl.type then
          continue
        unless decl.binderInfo.isExplicit do
          unless resultType.containsFVar x.fvarId! do
            throwError "deriving Encode: the implicit argument {decl.userName} of \
              {ctorName} is not determined by the type of the constructor"
          continue
        match xTy.getAppFn with
        | .const declName .. =>
          if declName == indVal.name then
            parts := parts.push (← `($(mkIdent ctx.auxFunNames[0]!) $a:ident))
          else
            parts := parts.push (← `(Encode.encode $a:ident))
        | _ => parts := parts.push (← `(Encode.encode $a:ident))
      patterns := patterns.push (← `(@$(mkIdent ctorName):ident $ctorArgs:term*))
      let rhs : Term ← if parts.isEmpty then `(([] : List Nat))
        else parts[1:].foldlM (fun acc p => `($acc ++ $p)) parts[0]!
      `(matchAltExpr| | $[$patterns:term],* => $rhs:term)
    alts := alts.push alt
  `(match $[$discrs],* with $alts:matchAlt*)

/-- The commands defining the encoding function of the inductive type
`declName` and its `Encode` instance. -/
def mkEncodeInstanceCmds (declName : Name) : TermElabM (Array Syntax) := do
  let ctx ← mkContext ``Encode "encode" declName
  if ctx.usePartial then
    throwError "deriving Encode: mutual and nested inductive types are not supported"
  let indVal := ctx.typeInfos[0]!
  let header ← mkHeader ``Encode 1 indVal
  let body ← mkEncodeMatch ctx header indVal
  let fn ← `(def $(mkIdent ctx.auxFunNames[0]!):ident $(header.binders):bracketedBinder* :
      List Nat := $body:term)
  return #[fn] ++ (← mkInstanceCmds ctx ``Encode #[declName])

/-- The deriving handler for `Encode`. -/
def mkEncodeHandler (declNames : Array Name) : CommandElabM Bool := do
  unless ← declNames.allM isInductive do
    return false
  for declName in declNames do
    let cmds ← liftTermElabM <| mkEncodeInstanceCmds declName
    cmds.forM elabCommand
  return true

initialize registerDerivingHandler ``Encode mkEncodeHandler

end Deriving

end Lax185574.Encoding

concepts.title: How inputs are given to algorithms
concepts.description:
The encodings of all values that algorithms in this submission read or
write. Except for lists, functions on `Fin n`, finite sets, graphs and
the values of ℕ∞, they are given by the rule of `Lax185574.Encoding`.
Encodings of further types, such as partial graphs and type trees, are
given next to their definitions.

| type | value | encoding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Bool` | `false`, `true` | `0`, `1` |
| `Fin n` | `i` | `i` |
| `α × β` | `(a, b)` | encoding of `a`, then of `b` |
| `α ⊕ β` | `inl a`, `inr b` | `0`, encoding of `a`, and `1`, encoding of `b` |
| `Option α` | `none`, `some a` | `0`, and `1`, encoding of `a` |
| `ℤ` | `m ≥ 0`, `-(m + 1)` | `0, m`, and `1, m` |
| `ℚ` | `p / q` in lowest terms, `q > 0` | `p` as an integer, then `q` |
| `ℕ∞` | `d`, `∞` | `d + 1`, and `0` |
| `Empty` | (no values) | |
| `List α` | `[a₁, …, aₘ]` | `m`, then the encodings of `a₁`, …, `aₘ` |
| `Fin n → α` | `f` | the list `[f 0, …, f (n - 1)]` |
| `Finset α` | `S` | the list of the encodings of the elements of `S`, in increasing order |

The encodings of the elements of a finite set are lists of numbers, and
they are compared lexicographically. As a list of lists, the encoding
of a set gives the length of each element's encoding in front of it.

A first-order formula is written in prefix (Polish) notation, with one
number per connective.

| formula | encoding |
| --- | --- |
| xᵢ adjacent to xⱼ | `0, i, j` |
| xᵢ = xⱼ | `1, i, j` |
| ¬φ | `2`, encoding of φ |
| φ ∧ ψ | `3`, encoding of φ, encoding of ψ |
| ∃xₙ φ | `4`, encoding of φ |
| xᵢ has color c | `5`, encoding of `c`, `i` |

The first-order formulas `Lax3.FirstOrder.FO` of the archive, which
have no colors, are encoded in the same way, `0, i, j` for adjacency,
`1, i, j` for equality, and `2`, `3`, `4` for negation, conjunction and
the quantifier.

A graph with n vertices is encoded by the family of the neighborhoods of
its vertices 0, 1, …, n − 1, each a finite set of vertices. So the
encoding starts with n, followed for each vertex by its degree and its
neighbors in increasing order, each neighbor preceded by `1`, the length
of its encoding. A graph with n vertices and m edges has an encoding of
length n + 4m + 1, whose numbers are at most n. A graph of mathlib on
the vertices 0, 1, …, n − 1, a `SimpleGraph (Fin n)`, is encoded in the
same way.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The tables are not part of the definition. They spell out what the
instances below and `deriving Encode` write for these declarations.

The adjacency of a graph is a relation, so the encoding of a graph is not
derived. A number or ∞ takes one entry, so that a matrix of distances
has entries of constant size. Its derived encoding, as an optional
number, would take two entries for a finite value. Every finite set has exactly one encoding, so every graph has
exactly one encoding. Its length is at least the number of vertices, so
an algorithm whose running time is measured in the number of vertices
can read its whole input.

namespace Lax185574.Encodings

open Lax185574.Encoding Lax185574.Graphs Lax185574.FirstOrderLogic

universe u

deriving instance Encode for Bool, Fin, Prod, Sum, Option, Int, Rat, Empty, Formula,
  Lax3.FirstOrder.FO

/-- A list is encoded by its length, followed by the encodings of its
entries. -/
instance {α : Type u} [Encode α] : Encode (List α) where
  encode l := l.length :: (l.map encode).flatten

/-- A family indexed by `Fin n` is encoded as the list of its members. -/
instance {α : Type u} {n : ℕ} [Encode α] : Encode (Fin n → α) where
  encode f := encode (List.ofFn f)

/-- A finite set is encoded by the list of the encodings of its elements,
in increasing lexicographic order. -/
instance {α : Type u} [Encode α] : Encode (Finset α) where
  encode S := encode ((S.image encode).sort (· ≤ ·))

/-- A number `d` or `∞` is encoded as one number, `d + 1` for `d` and
`0` for `∞`. -/
instance : Encode ℕ∞ where
  encode d := [if d = ⊤ then 0 else d.toNat + 1]

open Classical in
/-- A graph of mathlib on `Fin n` is encoded by the family of the
neighborhoods of its vertices. -/
noncomputable instance {n : ℕ} : Encode (SimpleGraph (Fin n)) where
  encode H := encode fun v : Fin n => Finset.univ.filter (H.Adj v)

open Classical in
/-- A graph is encoded by the family of the neighborhoods of its
vertices. -/
noncomputable instance : Encode Graph where
  encode G := encode fun v : Fin G.n => ({u | G.Adj v u} : Finset (Fin G.n))

end Lax185574.Encodings

concepts.title: Evaluation of distance formulas on type trees
concepts.description:
Let φ(x̄) be a distFO formula of distance rank (k, q), G a partial graph
and ā ∈ V(G)^ℓ with ℓ = |x̄| ≤ k. Then whether G ⊨ φ(ā) holds is
decidable in polynomial time, given tree^G_{k,q}(ā) and φ.

For a type tree τ = tree^G_{k,q}(ā) one writes τ ⊨ φ if G ⊨ φ(ā). The
lemma shows that this depends on τ only.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The algorithm is an algorithm in the sense of `Lax185574.Algorithms`,
one for all k and q. Its input is the pair of the type tree and the
formula. It decides whether `u` satisfies `φ` in time polynomial in the
size of the input, `O((N + 1)^a)` for an input of length `N`. The
degree `a` and the constant `c` may depend on k and q. The paper says
polynomial time, with no subscript, so this is weaker than a degree
independent of k and q. It suffices, since k and q are fixed in every
use. Running times of the paper of the form poly_{k,q} are formalized
in the same way. That the answer depends on τ alone is part of the
statement, because the output of the algorithm depends on its input
only.

namespace Lax185574.Evaluation

open Lax185574.Encoding Lax185574.Algorithms
open Lax185574.PartialGraphs Lax185574.DistanceLogic Lax185574.DistanceLogic.DistFO
open Lax185574.TypeTrees

/-- **Evaluation.** One algorithm decides, given `tree_{k,q}(u)` and a
formula `φ` of distance rank `(k, q)`, whether `u` satisfies `φ`, in
time polynomial in the size of the input. -/
axiom exists_program_eval :
    ∃ A : Algorithm, ∀ k q : ℕ, ∃ c a : ℕ,
      ∀ (n : ℕ) (G : PartialGraph (Fin n)) (ℓ : ℕ) (u : Fin ℓ → Fin n) (φ : DistFO ℓ),
        ℓ ≤ k → DRank k q φ →
          A.Decides c (tree G k q u, φ) (Sat G u φ)
            (((encode (tree G k q u)).length + (encode φ).length + 1) ^ a)

end Lax185574.Evaluation

  ∀ (k q : Nat),
    Exists fun c =>
      Exists fun a =>
        ∀ (n : Nat) (G : Lax185574.PartialGraphs.PartialGraph (Fin n)) (ℓ : Nat) (u : Fin ℓ → Fin n)
          (φ : Lax185574.DistanceLogic.DistFO ℓ),

            Lax185574.DistanceLogic.DistFO.DRank k q φ →
              A.Decides c { fst := Lax185574.TypeTrees.tree G k q u, snd := φ }
                (Lax185574.DistanceLogic.DistFO.Sat G u φ)
                (instHPow.hPow
                  (instHAdd.hAdd
                    (instHAdd.hAdd
                      (Lax185574.TypeTrees.instEncodeTypeTree.encode (Lax185574.TypeTrees.tree G k q u)).length.cast
                      (Lax185574.DistanceLogic.instEncodeDistFO.encode φ).length.cast)
                    1)
                  a)

concepts.title: Far composition of type trees
concepts.description:
There is an operation ∗ on type trees such that for all k, q ∈ ℕ,
partial graphs G and nonempty tuples ā₁, ā₂ with |ā₁ ā₂| ≤ k and
dist(ā₁, ā₂) > ρ⁻(k, q),

  tree_{k,q}(ā₁) ∗ tree_{k,q}(ā₂) = tree_{k,q}(ā₁ ā₂).

Given τ₁ and τ₂ one can compute τ₁ ∗ τ₂ in time poly_{k,q}(‖τ₁‖ + ‖τ₂‖).

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The paper adapts Lemma 3.1 of its locality note. The operation is given
by one algorithm in the sense of `Lax185574.Algorithms`, for all k and
q, whose input is the pair of the two trees. The size ‖τ‖ is the length
of the encoding of τ, and the time is `O((‖τ₁‖ + ‖τ₂‖ + 1)^a)`, where the
degree `a` and the constant `c` may depend on k and q.
dist(ā₁, ā₂) > r means that no entry of ā₁ is within distance r of an
entry of ā₂.

namespace Lax185574.FarComposition

open Lax185574.Encoding Lax185574.Algorithms
open Lax185574.PartialGraphs Lax185574.GaifmanGraph Lax185574.TypeTrees
open Lax3.DistFO (rhoMinus rhoPlus)

/-- **Far composition.** One algorithm computes the type tree of the
concatenation of two far tuples from their type trees, in time
polynomial in their sizes. -/
axiom exists_program_compose :
    ∃ A : Algorithm, ∀ k q : ℕ, ∃ c a : ℕ,
      ∀ (n : ℕ) (G : PartialGraph (Fin n)) (ℓ₁ ℓ₂ : ℕ) (u₁ : Fin ℓ₁ → Fin n)

            (((encode (tree G k q u₁)).length + (encode (tree G k q u₂)).length + 1) ^ a)

end Lax185574.FarComposition

concepts.title: The far tree
concepts.description:
For a partial graph G, k ∈ ℕ, q ≥ 1 and a nonempty tuple ā of at most k
vertices,

  ftree_{k,q}(ā) = {tree_{k+1,q−1}(b) | b ∈ V(G), dist(ā, b) > ρ⁻(k+1, q−1)}.

It is the set of type trees of the vertices far from ā.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
dist(ā, b) > r means that no entry of ā is within distance r of b. The
far tree is a finite set of type trees. It is encoded as the sorted list
of the words of its trees, like the sets inside a type tree.

import Lax185574.TypeTrees

/-!
---
title: The far tree
type: definition
---
For a partial graph G, k ∈ ℕ, q ≥ 1 and a nonempty tuple ā of at most k
vertices,

  ftree_{k,q}(ā) = {tree_{k+1,q−1}(b) | b ∈ V(G), dist(ā, b) > ρ⁻(k+1, q−1)}.

It is the set of type trees of the vertices far from ā.

# Formalization notes

dist(ā, b) > r means that no entry of ā is within distance r of b. The
far tree is a finite set of type trees. It is encoded as the sorted list
of the words of its trees, like the sets inside a type tree.
-/

namespace Lax185574.FarTrees

open Lax185574.PartialGraphs Lax185574.GaifmanGraph
open Lax185574.TypeTrees
open Lax3.DistFO (rhoMinus rhoPlus)

variable {V : Type*}

/-- `ftree_{k,q}(a)`: the type trees of the vertices far from `a`. -/
noncomputable def ftree (G : PartialGraph V) (k q : ℕ) {ℓ : ℕ} (a : Fin ℓ → V) :
    Finset TypeTree :=
  finsetOf {ν | ∃ b : V,
    (∀ i, ¬ WithinDist G.resolved (rhoMinus (k + 1) (q - 1)) (a i) b) ∧
    ν = tree G (k + 1) (q - 1) ![b]}

end Lax185574.FarTrees

concepts.title: Construction sequences with few realized types
concepts.description:
Let 𝒞 be a monadically dependent graph class, r, q ∈ ℕ, and let ε > 0
be a rational. There is a constant α ≥ 1 depending only on 𝒞 and q such
that every graph G ∈ 𝒞 has a construction sequence of radius-r depth-q
width O_{𝒞,r,q,ε}(n^{αε}) and length O_{𝒞,r,q,ε}(n^{1+αε}). Moreover,

construction sequence in time Ô_{𝒞,r,q,ε}(n³). Here Ô_k(n³) stands for

title: Construction sequences with few realized types

namespace Lax185574.FewTypes

open Lax185574.Graphs Lax185574.MonadicDependence Lax185574.Algorithms
open Lax185574.ConstructionSequences Lax185574.Width

/-- **Construction sequences with few realized types.** One algorithm
computes, from `r`, `q`, a rational `ε > 0` and a graph `G`, a
construction sequence of `G`, given by its script. On members of a
monadically dependent class it takes time `O(n^(3+η))` for every
`η > 0`, and the sequence has length at most `c · (n+1)^(1+aε)` and
radius-`r` depth-`q` width at most `c · (n+1)^(aε)`. Here `a ≥ 1`
depends only on the class and `q`, and `c` on the class, `r`, `q`, `ε`
and `η`. -/
axiom exists_program_fewTypes :
    ∃ (A : Algorithm) (script : ℕ → ℕ → ℚ → (G : Graph) → Script G.n),
      (∀ (r q : ℕ) (ε : ℚ) (G : Graph), 0 < ε →
        IsConstructionSequence G.toSimpleGraph (script r q ε G).run ∧
          (script r q ε G).HasSmallNumbers) ∧
      ∀ C : GraphClass, MonadicallyDependent C → ∀ q : ℕ, ∃ a : ℕ, 1 ≤ a ∧
        ∀ (r : ℕ) (ε : ℚ), 0 < ε → ∀ η : ℝ, 0 < η → ∃ c : ℕ,
          ∀ G ∈ C,
            A.Computes c (r, q, ε, G) (script r q ε G) ((G.n : ℝ) ^ (3 + η)) ∧
            ((script r q ε G).run.length : ℝ) ≤ c * ((G.n : ℝ) + 1) ^ (1 + (a : ℝ) * ε) ∧
            (width r q (script r q ε G).run : ℝ) ≤ c * ((G.n : ℝ) + 1) ^ ((a : ℝ) * ε)

end Lax185574.FewTypes

concepts.title: First-order logic on colored graphs
concepts.description:
First-order formulas speak about the vertices of a graph. Their atoms
say that two vertices are adjacent, that they are equal, or that a
vertex has a color. Formulas are closed under negation, conjunction and
existential quantification over vertices. The other connectives and the
universal quantifier are expressed by these as usual.

A formula has free variables x₀, …, x_{n−1} for some n, and its
quantifier ∃ binds the next variable xₙ. A *sentence* has no free
variables and no colors, and `G ⊨ φ` says that the sentence φ holds in
the graph G.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The colors are the elements of a type `K`. Sentences use the empty type
of colors. A coloring of a graph assigns to each color the set of
vertices that have it, and the sets of different colors may overlap.

The type of a formula records how many free variables it may use, so a
formula cannot refer to a variable that is not bound or assigned.
Variables are numbered by the order in which they are introduced (de
Bruijn levels), so a variable keeps its number under a quantifier, and
`Fin.snoc a v` extends the assignment `a` of x₀, …, x_{n−1} by the vertex
`v` for xₙ.

concepts.sourceText:
import Lax185574.Graphs
import Mathlib.Data.Fin.Tuple.Basic

/-!
---
title: First-order logic on colored graphs
type: definition
---
First-order formulas speak about the vertices of a graph. Their atoms
say that two vertices are adjacent, that they are equal, or that a
vertex has a color. Formulas are closed under negation, conjunction and
existential quantification over vertices. The other connectives and the
universal quantifier are expressed by these as usual.

A formula has free variables x₀, …, x_{n−1} for some n, and its
quantifier ∃ binds the next variable xₙ. A *sentence* has no free
variables and no colors, and `G ⊨ φ` says that the sentence φ holds in
the graph G.

# Formalization notes

The colors are the elements of a type `K`. Sentences use the empty type
of colors. A coloring of a graph assigns to each color the set of
vertices that have it, and the sets of different colors may overlap.

The type of a formula records how many free variables it may use, so a
formula cannot refer to a variable that is not bound or assigned.
Variables are numbered by the order in which they are introduced (de
Bruijn levels), so a variable keeps its number under a quantifier, and
`Fin.snoc a v` extends the assignment `a` of x₀, …, x_{n−1} by the vertex
`v` for xₙ.
-/

namespace Lax185574.FirstOrderLogic

open Lax185574.Graphs

/-- First-order formulas on graphs with colors from `K`, whose free
variables are among `x₀, …, x_{n-1}`. -/
inductive Formula (K : Type) : ℕ → Type
  /-- `xᵢ` and `xⱼ` are adjacent. -/
  | adj {n : ℕ} (i j : Fin n) : Formula K n
  /-- `xᵢ` and `xⱼ` are equal. -/
  | eq {n : ℕ} (i j : Fin n) : Formula K n
  /-- Negation. -/
  | not {n : ℕ} (φ : Formula K n) : Formula K n
  /-- Conjunction. -/
  | and {n : ℕ} (φ ψ : Formula K n) : Formula K n
  /-- `∃ xₙ φ`: some vertex can be assigned to `xₙ` so that `φ` holds. -/
  | ex {n : ℕ} (φ : Formula K (n + 1)) : Formula K n
  /-- `xᵢ` has the color `c`. -/
  | color {n : ℕ} (c : K) (i : Fin n) : Formula K n

/-- The formula `φ` holds in the graph `G` with the coloring `col`, when
the free variable `xᵢ` is assigned the vertex `a i`. -/
def Formula.Holds {K : Type} (G : Graph) (col : K → Set (Fin G.n)) :
    {n : ℕ} → Formula K n → (Fin n → Fin G.n) → Prop
  | _, .adj i j, a => G.Adj (a i) (a j)
  | _, .eq i j, a => a i = a j
  | _, .not φ, a => ¬ φ.Holds G col a
  | _, .and φ ψ, a => φ.Holds G col a ∧ ψ.Holds G col a
  | _, .ex φ, a => ∃ v : Fin G.n, φ.Holds G col (Fin.snoc a v)
  | _, .color c i, a => a i ∈ col c

/-- A sentence: a formula without colors and without free variables. -/
abbrev Sentence : Type := Formula Empty 0

/-- The sentence `φ` holds in the graph `G`. -/
def Models (G : Graph) (φ : Sentence) : Prop :=
  φ.Holds G Empty.elim Fin.elim0

@[inherit_doc] scoped infix:50 " ⊨ " => Models

end Lax185574.FirstOrderLogic

concepts.title: Types of bounded quantifier rank
concepts.description:
Let A be a structure and W a set of its elements. A formula with
parameters from W is a formula in the signature of A expanded by a
constant for every element of W. For a tuple v̄ ∈ V(A)^k and q ∈ ℕ, the
*type of quantifier rank q of v̄ over W*, written tp_q(v̄/W), is the set
of all formulas φ(x₁, …, x_k) with parameters from W and of quantifier
rank at most q such that A ⊨ φ(v̄).

For sets X, Y of elements,
Types_{k,q}(X/Y) = { tp_q(v̄/Y) : v̄ ∈ X^k }
is the set of types realized by k-tuples from X. The notation omits /Y
when Y is empty, and then the types are those without parameters,
tp_q(v̄) and Types_{k,q}(X). The number of realized types |Types_{k,q}(X/Y)| is the
quantity that the paper bounds throughout.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
Types without parameters, `rankType` and `types`, are defined separately
from types over a parameter set, `rankTypeOver` and `typesOver`. Over
the empty set the two agree up to the evident bijection of formulas.
The separate version is needed because the formula type of the
parameterized version depends on the parameter set, so it would not
let one compare types in different structures, such as two induced
substructures.

Formulas are those of mathlib's first-order logic, `L.Formula α`, where
`α` indexes the free variables. A parameter from `W` is a free variable
of the right summand of `Fin k ⊕ W`, and it is always assigned the
element that it names. This is the same as adjoining a constant for each
element of `W`, and it does not change the quantifier rank. The type is
literally the set of formulas, as in the paper, and the count is the
cardinality of the set of realized types. It is finite whenever `X` is
finite, since it is the image of `X^k`.

The count `typeCountOver` takes the structure as an explicit argument,
because it is applied to structures that are not instances, such as the
expansion of a graph by colors.

Mathlib's formulas are built from falsum, equality, relations,
implication and universal quantification. The quantifier rank is the
nesting depth of the universal quantifier. Every formula of the usual
syntax with ¬, ∧, ∨, ∃ and ∀ translates into this syntax without
changing its quantifier rank, so the types are the usual ones.

/-!
---
title: Types of bounded quantifier rank
type: definition
---
Let A be a structure and W a set of its elements. A formula with
parameters from W is a formula in the signature of A expanded by a

*type of quantifier rank q of v̄ over W*, written tp_q(v̄/W), is the set
of all formulas φ(x₁, …, x_k) with parameters from W and of quantifier
rank at most q such that A ⊨ φ(v̄).

For sets X, Y of elements,
Types_{k,q}(X/Y) = { tp_q(v̄/Y) : v̄ ∈ X^k }
is the set of types realized by k-tuples from X. The notation omits /Y
when Y is empty, and then the types are those without parameters,
tp_q(v̄) and Types_{k,q}(X). The number of realized types |Types_{k,q}(X/Y)| is the
quantity that the paper bounds throughout.

# Formalization notes

Types without parameters, `rankType` and `types`, are defined separately
from types over a parameter set, `rankTypeOver` and `typesOver`. Over
the empty set the two agree up to the evident bijection of formulas.
The separate version is needed because the formula type of the
parameterized version depends on the parameter set, so it would not
let one compare types in different structures, such as two induced
substructures.

Formulas are those of mathlib's first-order logic, `L.Formula α`, where
`α` indexes the free variables. A parameter from `W` is a free variable
of the right summand of `Fin k ⊕ W`, and it is always assigned the
element that it names. This is the same as adjoining a constant for each
element of `W`, and it does not change the quantifier rank. The type is
literally the set of formulas, as in the paper, and the count is the
cardinality of the set of realized types. It is finite whenever `X` is
finite, since it is the image of `X^k`.

The count `typeCountOver` takes the structure as an explicit argument,
because it is applied to structures that are not instances, such as the
expansion of a graph by colors.

Mathlib's formulas are built from falsum, equality, relations,
implication and universal quantification. The quantifier rank is the

syntax with ¬, ∧, ∨, ∃ and ∀ translates into this syntax without
changing its quantifier rank, so the types are the usual ones.
-/

namespace Lax185574.FirstOrderTypes

open FirstOrder FirstOrder.Language

universe u v w z

variable {L : Language.{u, v}}

/-- The quantifier rank of a formula: the nesting depth of its
quantifiers. -/
def quantifierRank {α : Type w} : {n : ℕ} → L.BoundedFormula α n → ℕ
  | _, .falsum => 0
  | _, .equal _ _ => 0
  | _, .rel _ _ => 0
  | _, .imp φ ψ => max (quantifierRank φ) (quantifierRank ψ)
  | _, .all φ => quantifierRank φ + 1

variable {V : Type z}

section

variable [L.Structure V]

/-- The type `tp_q(v̄)` of quantifier rank `q` of the tuple `v`: the
formulas of quantifier rank at most `q`, without parameters, that hold
of `v`. -/
def rankType (q : ℕ) {k : ℕ} (v : Fin k → V) : Set (L.Formula (Fin k)) :=
  {φ | quantifierRank φ ≤ q ∧ φ.Realize v}

/-- `Types_{k,q}(X)`: the types of quantifier rank `q` of the `k`-tuples
from `X`. -/
def types (k q : ℕ) (X : Set V) : Set (Set (L.Formula (Fin k))) :=
  rankType q '' {v : Fin k → V | ∀ i, v i ∈ X}

/-- `|Types_{k,q}(X)|`: the number of types of quantifier rank `q`
realized by `k`-tuples from `X`. -/
noncomputable def typeCount (k q : ℕ) (X : Set V) : ℕ :=
  (types (L := L) k q X).ncard

/-- The type `tp_q(v̄/W)` of quantifier rank `q` of the tuple `v` over
the parameter set `W`: the formulas of quantifier rank at most `q` with
parameters from `W` that hold of `v`. -/
def rankTypeOver (q : ℕ) (W : Set V) {k : ℕ} (v : Fin k → V) :
    Set (L.Formula (Fin k ⊕ W)) :=
  {φ | quantifierRank φ ≤ q ∧ φ.Realize (Sum.elim v Subtype.val)}

/-- `Types_{k,q}(X/Y)`: the types of quantifier rank `q` over `Y` of the
`k`-tuples from `X`. -/
def typesOver (k q : ℕ) (X Y : Set V) : Set (Set (L.Formula (Fin k ⊕ Y))) :=
  rankTypeOver q Y '' {v : Fin k → V | ∀ i, v i ∈ X}

end

/-- `|Types_{k,q}(X/Y)|`: the number of types of quantifier rank `q` over
`Y` realized by `k`-tuples from `X`, in the structure `M`. -/
noncomputable def typeCountOver (M : L.Structure V) (k q : ℕ) (X Y : Set V) : ℕ :=
  (@typesOver L V M k q X Y).ncard

end Lax185574.FirstOrderTypes

concepts.title: Refining a partition increases the flip metric
concepts.description:
If 𝒬 refines 𝒫, then every 𝒫-flip is also a 𝒬-flip, and hence

dist_𝒬(u, v) ≥ dist_𝒫(u, v).

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
Refinement is 𝒬 ≤ 𝒫 for setoids. The inequality of the flip metrics is
stated through their balls: for every r, Ball^𝒬_r(v) ⊆ Ball^𝒫_r(v),
that is, dist_𝒬(u, v) ≤ r implies dist_𝒫(u, v) ≤ r. This is the
inequality for distances that may be infinite. The two parts of the
observation are two axioms. The graph may be infinite.

/-- If `𝒬` refines `𝒫`, every `𝒫`-flip is a `𝒬`-flip. -/

    (hQP : Q ≤ P) (H : SimpleGraph V) (hH : IsFlip G P H) : IsFlip G Q H

/-- If `𝒬` refines `𝒫`, then `dist_𝒬(u, v) ≥ dist_𝒫(u, v)`: every ball
of the flip metric of `𝒬` lies in the ball of the same radius of the

concepts.title: Flips and flip metrics
concepts.description:
For a graph G and a partition 𝒫 of V ≔ V(G), a *𝒫-flip* of G is a graph
H with V(H) = V such that for every pair X, Y ∈ 𝒫 (possibly X = Y),
either H[X, Y] = G[X, Y] or H[X, Y] = Ḡ[X, Y]. If |𝒫| ≤ s, then H is
an *s-flip* of G. The associated *flip metric* and its balls are

dist_𝒫(u, v) ≔ max { dist^H(u, v) : H is a 𝒫-flip of G },
Ball^𝒫_r(v) ≔ { u : dist_𝒫(u, v) ≤ r } = ⋂ { Ball^H_r(v) : H is a 𝒫-flip of G }.

As a shorthand, for a graph G and a set S ⊆ V(G), a 𝒫_S-flip of G is
called an *S-flip*, and dist_S^G ≔ dist_{𝒫_S} and Ball^S_r ≔ Ball^{𝒫_S}_r.
Here 𝒫_S is the partition into atomic types over S, see
`Lax185574.AtomicTypes` and `Lax185574.Partitions`.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
"H[X, Y] = G[X, Y] or H[X, Y] = Ḡ[X, Y]" says that on all pairs of
distinct vertices x ∈ X, y ∈ Y, adjacency in H agrees with adjacency in
G, or on all of them it agrees with non-adjacency in G. For X = Y this
reads H[X] = G[X] or H[X] = Ḡ[X], which is the intended meaning. The
parts X and Y are named by vertices a and b with X = 𝒫(a) and Y = 𝒫(b).

The bound dist_𝒫(u, v) ≤ r is `FlipWithinDist`: in every 𝒫-flip, some
walk from u to v has length at most r. Distances are measured by walks,
as in `Lax185574.GaifmanGraph`, so the maximum of the paper is never
needed as a number, and an infinite distance in some flip is allowed.
The ball is the set of vertices u with dist_𝒫(v, u) ≤ r, which is the
intersection form of the paper. The ball Ball^S_r(v) is
`flipBall G (atomicTypes G S) r v` and gets no separate name. An s-flip
is a 𝒫-flip with `Nat.card (Quotient 𝒫) ≤ s`, which is spelled out where
it is used.

type: definition
---
For a graph G and a partition 𝒫 of V ≔ V(G), a *𝒫-flip* of G is a graph
H with V(H) = V such that for every pair X, Y ∈ 𝒫 (possibly X = Y),
either H[X, Y] = G[X, Y] or H[X, Y] = Ḡ[X, Y]. If |𝒫| ≤ s, then H is
an *s-flip* of G. The associated *flip metric* and its balls are

dist_𝒫(u, v) ≔ max { dist^H(u, v) : H is a 𝒫-flip of G },
Ball^𝒫_r(v) ≔ { u : dist_𝒫(u, v) ≤ r } = ⋂ { Ball^H_r(v) : H is a 𝒫-flip of G }.

As a shorthand, for a graph G and a set S ⊆ V(G), a 𝒫_S-flip of G is
called an *S-flip*, and dist_S^G ≔ dist_{𝒫_S} and Ball^S_r ≔ Ball^{𝒫_S}_r.
Here 𝒫_S is the partition into atomic types over S, see
`Lax185574.AtomicTypes` and `Lax185574.Partitions`.

# Formalization notes

"H[X, Y] = G[X, Y] or H[X, Y] = Ḡ[X, Y]" says that on all pairs of
distinct vertices x ∈ X, y ∈ Y, adjacency in H agrees with adjacency in
G, or on all of them it agrees with non-adjacency in G. For X = Y this
reads H[X] = G[X] or H[X] = Ḡ[X], which is the intended meaning. The
parts X and Y are named by vertices a and b with X = 𝒫(a) and Y = 𝒫(b).

The bound dist_𝒫(u, v) ≤ r is `FlipWithinDist`: in every 𝒫-flip, some
walk from u to v has length at most r. Distances are measured by walks,
as in `Lax185574.GaifmanGraph`, so the maximum of the paper is never
needed as a number, and an infinite distance in some flip is allowed.
The ball is the set of vertices u with dist_𝒫(v, u) ≤ r, which is the
intersection form of the paper. The ball Ball^S_r(v) is
`flipBall G (atomicTypes G S) r v` and gets no separate name. An s-flip
is a 𝒫-flip with `Nat.card (Quotient 𝒫) ≤ s`, which is spelled out where
it is used.
-/

namespace Lax185574.Flips

open Lax185574.Partitions Lax185574.GaifmanGraph

universe z

variable {V : Type z}

/-- `H` is a `𝒫`-flip of `G`: for every pair of parts `𝒫(a)`, `𝒫(b)`,
adjacency in `H` between distinct vertices of these parts either agrees
with adjacency in `G` throughout, or with non-adjacency in `G`
throughout. -/
def IsFlip (G : SimpleGraph V) (P : Setoid V) (H : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∀ a b : V,
    (∀ x y : V, P x a → P y b → x ≠ y → (H.Adj x y ↔ G.Adj x y)) ∨
      (∀ x y : V, P x a → P y b → x ≠ y → (H.Adj x y ↔ ¬ G.Adj x y))

/-- `dist_𝒫(u, v) ≤ r`: in every `𝒫`-flip of `G`, some walk from `u`
to `v` has length at most `r`. -/
def FlipWithinDist (G : SimpleGraph V) (P : Setoid V) (r : ℕ) (u v : V) : Prop :=
  ∀ H : SimpleGraph V, IsFlip G P H → WithinDist H r u v

/-- `Ball^𝒫_r(v)`: the vertices within distance `r` of `v` in every
`𝒫`-flip of `G`. -/
def flipBall (G : SimpleGraph V) (P : Setoid V) (r : ℕ) (v : V) : Set V :=
  {u | FlipWithinDist G P r v u}

end Lax185574.Flips

concepts.description:
Let 𝒞 be a monadically dependent graph class and s ∈ ℕ. The class
consisting of all s-definable flips of graphs from 𝒞 is monadically

sections.title: Formalization notes

The paper allows infinite graphs in this part. Here the graphs are
those of a `GraphClass`, which are finite, as in every use.

namespace Lax185574.FlipsMonadicallyDependent

open Lax185574.Graphs Lax185574.MonadicDependence Lax185574.DefinableFlips

/-- The class of all `s`-definable flips of graphs from `C`. -/
def definableFlipClass (C : GraphClass) (s : ℕ) : GraphClass :=
  {H | ∃ G ∈ C, ∃ F : SimpleGraph (Fin G.n),
    IsDefinableFlip G.toSimpleGraph s F ∧ H = Graph.ofSimpleGraph F}

/-- **Definable flips preserve monadic dependence.** The `s`-definable
flips of the graphs of a monadically dependent class form a monadically
dependent class. -/
axiom monadicallyDependent_definableFlipClass (C : GraphClass)
    (hC : MonadicallyDependent C) (s : ℕ) :
    MonadicallyDependent (definableFlipClass C s)

end Lax185574.FlipsMonadicallyDependent

concepts.title: Gaifman graph, distances, balls and induced substructures
concepts.description:
The *Gaifman graph* of a relational structure A with domain V has
vertex set V. Two distinct elements are adjacent if they occur together
in some tuple of some relation of A. For a structure with unary and
binary relations, these are the pairs uv such that (u, v) or (v, u) lies
in a binary relation. The distance dist^A(u, v) is the distance in the
Gaifman graph, and Ball^A_r(ā) is the set of elements at distance at
most r from some entry of the tuple ā.

For a set B of elements of a relational structure A, the *induced
substructure* A[B] has domain B, and each relation of A is restricted
to B. The paper uses A[B] without defining it.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
"At distance at most r" is witnessed by a walk of length at most r, as
in `Lax3.ColoredGraphs`. Elements in different components are therefore
at infinite distance. The induced substructure is defined for relational
languages, where every subset is closed under the (absent) functions.
Its domain is the subtype of `B`.

import Mathlib.ModelTheory.Basic
import Mathlib.Combinatorics.SimpleGraph.Walk.Basic

/-!
---
title: Gaifman graph, distances, balls and induced substructures
type: definition
---
The *Gaifman graph* of a relational structure A with domain V has
vertex set V. Two distinct elements are adjacent if they occur together
in some tuple of some relation of A. For a structure with unary and
binary relations, these are the pairs uv such that (u, v) or (v, u) lies
in a binary relation. The distance dist^A(u, v) is the distance in the
Gaifman graph, and Ball^A_r(ā) is the set of elements at distance at
most r from some entry of the tuple ā.

For a set B of elements of a relational structure A, the *induced
substructure* A[B] has domain B, and each relation of A is restricted
to B. The paper uses A[B] without defining it.

# Formalization notes

"At distance at most r" is witnessed by a walk of length at most r, as
in `Lax3.ColoredGraphs`. Elements in different components are therefore
at infinite distance. The induced substructure is defined for relational
languages, where every subset is closed under the (absent) functions.
Its domain is the subtype of `B`.
-/

namespace Lax185574.GaifmanGraph

open FirstOrder FirstOrder.Language

universe u v z

variable {L : Language.{u, v}} {V : Type z} [L.Structure V]

variable (L) in
/-- The Gaifman graph: distinct elements are adjacent if they occur
together in a tuple of some relation. -/
def gaifmanGraph : SimpleGraph V :=
  SimpleGraph.fromRel fun a b =>
    ∃ (l : ℕ) (R : L.Relations l) (x : Fin l → V),
      Structure.RelMap R x ∧ a ∈ Set.range x ∧ b ∈ Set.range x

/-- The vertices `u` and `v` of the graph `G` are within distance `d`:
some walk from `u` to `v` has length at most `d`. -/
def WithinDist {W : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph W) (d : ℕ) (u v : W) : Prop :=
  ∃ p : G.Walk u v, p.length ≤ d

variable (L) in
/-- `Ball^A_r(ā)`: the elements within distance `r` of some entry of the
tuple `a` in the Gaifman graph. -/
def ball (r : ℕ) {k : ℕ} (a : Fin k → V) : Set V :=
  {b | ∃ i, WithinDist (gaifmanGraph L (V := V)) r (a i) b}

/-- The induced substructure `A[B]` of a relational structure: the
relations of `A`, restricted to `B`. -/
@[implicit_reducible]
def induced [L.IsRelational] (B : Set V) : L.Structure B where
  funMap f := isEmptyElim f
  RelMap R x := Structure.RelMap R (fun i => (x i : V))

end Lax185574.GaifmanGraph

concepts.title: Gaifman's locality theorem with a rank bound
concepts.description:
For all α, q, k ∈ ℕ there is a p = p(α, q, k), computable from α, q, k,
with the following property. Let σ be a finite relational signature of
arity at most α. Every σ-formula φ(x̄) of quantifier rank at most q and
with |x̄| ≤ k free variables is equivalent to a σ-formula φ^loc(x̄),
computable from φ, that is a Boolean combination of basic 7^q-local
sentences and 7^q-local formulas, each of quantifier rank at most p.

This is Gaifman's locality theorem. Gaifman's paper does not state the
bound p explicitly. An analysis of its proof shows that p depends only
on α, q and k, and not on the signature σ, as the rank-preserving locality theorems of Dreier and
Toruńczyk and of van Bergerem, Grohe and Schweikardt make explicit for
their variants of local formulas. The dependence of p on α comes from expressing the
distance predicates in plain first-order logic.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The number p is quantified before the signature, so it depends on α, q
and k only. A finite relational signature of arity at most α is a
relational language with finitely many relation symbols, none of arity
above α. The formula has exactly n free variables for some n ≤ k.

The Boolean combinations are those generated from the constituents by
falsum and implication, which give all Boolean connectives. A basic
local sentence becomes a formula with the free variables x̄ by the
evident relabelling of its (absent) free variables. Each constituent,
a 7^q-local formula or a basic 7^q-local sentence, has quantifier rank
at most p, counting the quantifiers of the dist formulas in the ball
guards. Equivalence is over all finite structures with domain in an arbitrary
universe, including the empty one. The theorem holds for all structures,
but its only use, `Lax185574.LocalToGlobal`, concerns finite ones.

The present paper asserts that p is computable from α, q, k and that
φ^loc is computable from φ. Here both only exist, since no algorithm uses them.

type: theorem
---

Toruńczyk and of van Bergerem, Grohe and Schweikardt make explicit for

# Formalization notes

namespace Lax185574.GaifmanLocality

open FirstOrder FirstOrder.Language
open Lax185574.FirstOrderTypes Lax185574.LocalFormulas

universe u v w z

variable {L : Language.{u, v}}

/-- `IsBooleanCombination P φ`: the formula `φ` is a Boolean combination
of formulas satisfying `P`, built by falsum and implication. -/
inductive IsBooleanCombination {α : Type w} (P : L.Formula α → Prop) :
    L.Formula α → Prop
  /-- A constituent is a Boolean combination. -/
  | atom {φ : L.Formula α} : P φ → IsBooleanCombination P φ
  /-- Falsum is a Boolean combination. -/
  | falsum : IsBooleanCombination P ⊥
  /-- Implications of Boolean combinations are Boolean combinations. -/
  | imp {φ ψ : L.Formula α} :
      IsBooleanCombination P φ → IsBooleanCombination P ψ →
        IsBooleanCombination P (φ.imp ψ)

/-- The constituents of a Gaifman normal form with radius `h` and rank
bound `p`: `h`-local formulas and basic `h`-local sentences, each of
quantifier rank at most `p`. -/
def IsLocalConstituent [Finite (Σ l, L.Relations l)] (h p : ℕ) {n : ℕ}
    (χ : L.Formula (Fin n)) : Prop :=
  (IsLocal h χ ∧ quantifierRank χ ≤ p) ∨
    ∃ ψ : L.Sentence, IsBasicLocal h ψ ∧ quantifierRank ψ ≤ p ∧
      χ = ψ.relabel Empty.elim

/-- **Gaifman's locality theorem.** For all `α, q, k` there is a rank
bound `p` such that every formula of quantifier rank at most `q` with at
most `k` free variables, over a finite relational signature of arity at
most `α`, is equivalent to a Boolean combination of `7^q`-local formulas
and basic `7^q`-local sentences of quantifier rank at most `p`. -/
axiom exists_local_equivalent (α q k : ℕ) :
    ∃ p : ℕ, ∀ (L : Language.{u, v}) [L.IsRelational] [Finite (Σ l, L.Relations l)],
      (∀ l, α < l → IsEmpty (L.Relations l)) →
      ∀ (n : ℕ), n ≤ k → ∀ φ : L.Formula (Fin n), quantifierRank φ ≤ q →
        ∃ ψ : L.Formula (Fin n), FinitelyEquivalent.{u, v, z, 0} φ ψ ∧
          IsBooleanCombination (IsLocalConstituent (7 ^ q) p) ψ

end Lax185574.GaifmanLocality

concepts.title: Balls around vertex sets in a graph
concepts.description:
For a graph G, a radius r ∈ ℕ and a set C ⊆ V(G), the ball

Ball^G_r[C] = { w ∈ V(G) : dist^G(c, w) ≤ r for some c ∈ C }

is the union of the balls Ball^G_r[c] of radius r around the vertices
c ∈ C. For a vertex v it is written Ball^G_r[v], and for a tuple v̄ it
is the ball around the set of entries of v̄.

The distance between two sets is the minimum distance between their
elements. So dist^G(X, A) > r holds if and only if Ball^G_r[X] is
disjoint from A.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The ball is defined for a simple graph and an arbitrary set of centers.
"Distance at most r" is `GaifmanGraph.WithinDist`, a walk of length at
most r. Vertices in different components are at infinite distance. The
paper writes the closed ball defined here as Ball^G_r(v).

Statements of the form dist^G(X, A) > r, for sets or for the entries of
a tuple, are expressed as disjointness of Ball^G_r[X] and A. This
matches the paper's own reformulation of separation as an empty
intersection of a ball with a set. If A is empty, the distance is
infinite and the condition holds.

/-- `Ball^G_r[C]`: the vertices within distance `r` of some vertex of
`C`. -/
def graphBall (G : SimpleGraph V) (r : ℕ) (C : Set V) : Set V :=
  {w | ∃ c ∈ C, WithinDist G r c w}

end Lax185574.GraphBalls

concepts.title: Graphs and graph classes
concepts.description:
A *graph* has the vertices 0, 1, …, n − 1 for some n and a symmetric
and irreflexive adjacency relation. A *graph class* is a set of graphs.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The vertex count is part of the graph, so that a graph class is simply
a set of graphs and a graph can be passed to an algorithm as one value.
The fields are those of mathlib's `SimpleGraph` on `Fin n`, written out
so that the definition can be read without knowing mathlib.

The notions of graph theory in this submission are stated for mathlib's
`SimpleGraph`, whose library they use. A graph is turned into one by
`Graph.toSimpleGraph`, which keeps the vertices and the adjacency.
Conversely, `Graph.ofSimpleGraph` turns a simple graph on the vertices
0, 1, …, n − 1 into a graph.

A graph class need not be closed under isomorphism. Every notion applied

concepts.sourceText:
import Mathlib.Combinatorics.SimpleGraph.Basic

/-!
---
title: Graphs and graph classes
type: definition
---
A *graph* has the vertices 0, 1, …, n − 1 for some n and a symmetric
and irreflexive adjacency relation. A *graph class* is a set of graphs.

# Formalization notes

The vertex count is part of the graph, so that a graph class is simply
a set of graphs and a graph can be passed to an algorithm as one value.
The fields are those of mathlib's `SimpleGraph` on `Fin n`, written out
so that the definition can be read without knowing mathlib.

The notions of graph theory in this submission are stated for mathlib's
`SimpleGraph`, whose library they use. A graph is turned into one by
`Graph.toSimpleGraph`, which keeps the vertices and the adjacency.
Conversely, `Graph.ofSimpleGraph` turns a simple graph on the vertices
0, 1, …, n − 1 into a graph.

A graph class need not be closed under isomorphism. Every notion applied
to graph classes in this submission is invariant under isomorphism
anyway.
-/

namespace Lax185574.Graphs

/-- A graph on the vertices `0, 1, …, n - 1`. -/
structure Graph where
  /-- The number of vertices. -/
  n : ℕ
  /-- The adjacency relation. -/
  Adj : Fin n → Fin n → Prop
  /-- Adjacency is symmetric. -/
  symm : ∀ u v, Adj u v → Adj v u
  /-- No vertex is adjacent to itself. -/
  loopless : ∀ v, ¬ Adj v v

/-- A graph class: a set of graphs. -/
abbrev GraphClass : Type := Set Graph

/-- The graph `G` as a mathlib `SimpleGraph` on its vertices
`0, 1, …, n - 1`, with the same adjacency. -/
def Graph.toSimpleGraph (G : Graph) : SimpleGraph (Fin G.n) where
  Adj := G.Adj
  symm := ⟨G.symm⟩
  loopless := ⟨G.loopless⟩

/-- The mathlib `SimpleGraph` `H` on the vertices `0, 1, …, n - 1` as a
graph, with the same adjacency. -/
def Graph.ofSimpleGraph {n : ℕ} (H : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) : Graph :=
  ⟨n, H.Adj, fun _ _ h => H.adj_symm h, fun _ => H.irrefl⟩

end Lax185574.Graphs

concepts.title: Splitting by a transversal gives a partition homogeneous modulo the pair relation
concepts.description:
Fix a graph G and a partition 𝒫 of V(G), let T be a transversal of 𝒫,
and R ≔ R(G, 𝒫). Then 𝒬 ≔ 𝒫 ∧ T is *homogeneous modulo R*, that is,
for all X, Y ∈ 𝒬 either

XY ∖ R ⊆ E(G)  or  XY ∖ R ⊆ E(Ḡ).

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
Homogeneity modulo R is `MergeSequences.HomogeneousModulo`, the fourth
condition of a merge sequence. The graph may be infinite.

title: Splitting by a transversal gives a partition homogeneous modulo the pair relation
type: lemma

and R ≔ R(G, 𝒫). Then 𝒬 ≔ 𝒫 ∧ T is *homogeneous modulo R*, that is,
for all X, Y ∈ 𝒬 either

XY ∖ R ⊆ E(G)  or  XY ∖ R ⊆ E(Ḡ).

# Formalization notes

/-- **Homogeneity modulo the pair relation.** For a transversal `T` of

axiom homogeneousModulo_split {V : Type z} (G : SimpleGraph V) (P : Setoid V) (T : Set V)

concepts.title: Monadic dependence through the independence property
concepts.description:
A formula φ(x, y) in the signature of colored graphs has the
*independence property* on a graph class 𝒞 if for every n there are a
coloring G⁺ of a graph G ∈ 𝒞, vertices a₁, …, aₙ, and vertices b_J for
J ⊆ [n] such that G⁺ ⊨ φ(aᵢ, b_J) holds exactly when i ∈ J. A class is
monadically dependent if and only if no formula has the independence
property on it.

By a result of Baldwin and Shelah, one may equivalently allow formulas
φ(x̄, ȳ) with tuples of variables, and tuples āᵢ and b̄_J. On a
monadically dependent class, no such formula has the independence
property either.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The paper defines monadic dependence by transductions, like
`Lax185574.MonadicDependence`, and states the characterization by the
independence property as a theorem of Baldwin and Shelah, in its
appendix on forbidden patterns. The first statement of this concept is
this characterization for formulas in two single variables. The second
is the tuple form, in the direction the paper uses.

Formulas and colorings are those of `Lax185574.FirstOrderLogic`. A
formula φ(x̄, ȳ) has the free variables x₀, …, x_{p+p'−1}. The first p
of them form the tuple x̄ and the last p' form ȳ. The assignment
`Fin.append ā b̄` gives x̄ the values ā and ȳ the values b̄, which is the
paper's φ(ā, b̄). A formula φ(x, y) in two single variables is the case
p = p' = 1, written `1 + 1`.

import Lax185574.MonadicDependence

/-!

title: Monadic dependence through the independence property
type: theorem
---

φ(x̄, ȳ) with tuples of variables, and tuples āᵢ and b̄_J. On a
monadically dependent class, no such formula has the independence
property either.

# Formalization notes

The paper defines monadic dependence by transductions, like
`Lax185574.MonadicDependence`, and states the characterization by the
independence property as a theorem of Baldwin and Shelah, in its
appendix on forbidden patterns. The first statement of this concept is
this characterization for formulas in two single variables. The second
is the tuple form, in the direction the paper uses.

Formulas and colorings are those of `Lax185574.FirstOrderLogic`. A

-/

namespace Lax185574.IndependenceProperty

open Lax185574.Graphs Lax185574.FirstOrderLogic Lax185574.MonadicDependence

/-- The formula `φ(x̄, ȳ)` with `k` colors, whose free variables are a
tuple `x̄` of `p` variables followed by a tuple `ȳ` of `p'` variables,
has the *independence property* on `C`: for every `m` there are a graph
`G ∈ C`, a coloring of `G`, tuples `a i` for `i < m` and tuples `b J`
for `J ⊆ {0, …, m - 1}` such that `φ(a i, b J)` holds exactly when
`i ∈ J`. -/
def HasIP (C : GraphClass) {k p p' : ℕ} (φ : Formula (Fin k) (p + p')) : Prop :=
  ∀ m : ℕ, ∃ G ∈ C, ∃ (col : Fin k → Set (Fin G.n)) (a : Fin m → Fin p → Fin G.n)
    (b : Finset (Fin m) → Fin p' → Fin G.n),
    ∀ (i : Fin m) (J : Finset (Fin m)), φ.Holds G col (Fin.append (a i) (b J)) ↔ i ∈ J

/-- A graph class is monadically dependent if and only if no formula
`φ(x, y)` of colored graphs, in two single variables, has the
independence property on it. -/
axiom monadicallyDependent_iff_forall_not_hasIP (C : GraphClass) :
    MonadicallyDependent C ↔ ∀ (k : ℕ) (φ : Formula (Fin k) (1 + 1)), ¬ HasIP C φ

/-- On a monadically dependent class, no formula `φ(x̄, ȳ)` of colored
graphs, in tuples of variables, has the independence property
(Baldwin–Shelah). -/
axiom not_hasIP_of_monadicallyDependent (C : GraphClass) (hC : MonadicallyDependent C)
    {k p p' : ℕ} (φ : Formula (Fin k) (p + p')) : ¬ HasIP C φ

end Lax185574.IndependenceProperty

concepts.title: Locally definable construction sequences
concepts.description:
Let A be a structure and H a partial graph with V(H) ⊆ V(A). Then H is
*definable* in A by formulas of quantifier rank q₀ with parameters from
a set S ⊆ V(A) if for every relation R of H of arity k there is a formula
φ_R(x₁, …, x_k) of quantifier rank at most q₀ with parameters from S
such that, for all v̄ ∈ V(A)^k,

A ⊨ φ_R(v̄)  ⟺  v̄ ∈ V(H)^k and H ⊨ R(v̄).

Let G be a graph and r, c, s, q₀ ∈ ℕ. A construction sequence
G₁, …, G_λ of G is *radius-r definable* with c unary predicates,
s parameters and quantifier rank q₀ if, for all t ∈ [λ−1] and
v ∈ V(G), the induced partial graph G_t[Ball^{G_{t+1}}_r(v)] is
definable in some expansion of G by c unary predicates, by formulas of
quantifier rank q₀ with parameters from a set of at most s vertices.
The expansion and the parameters may depend on t and v.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The defined partial graph is an induced partial graph H[B]. It is given
by H and the set B, so the definition needs no subtype. Its relations
are those of H restricted to B. The condition "v̄ ∈ V(H[B])^k and
H[B] ⊨ R(v̄)" therefore reads "every entry of v̄ lies in B and H ⊨ R(v̄)".
The relations are the edges, the non-edges and every color class. A
color class that misses B is defined by any false formula, so only
finitely many conditions have content. Parameters are free variables of
the right summand, as in `Lax185574.FirstOrderTypes`.

import Lax185574.ConstructionSequences

namespace Lax185574.LocalDefinability

open FirstOrder FirstOrder.Language
open Lax185574.PartialGraphs Lax185574.FirstOrderTypes Lax185574.Colorings
open Lax710763.Transductions

universe u v z

variable {V : Type z}

/-- The induced partial graph `H[B]` is definable in the structure on
`V` by formulas of quantifier rank at most `q₀` with parameters from
`S`. -/
def DefinableIn {L : Language.{u, v}} [L.Structure V] (q₀ : ℕ) (S : Set V)
    (H : PartialGraph V) (B : Set V) : Prop :=
  ∀ {k : ℕ} (R : PartialGraphs.language.Relations k),
    ∃ φ : L.Formula (Fin k ⊕ S), quantifierRank φ ≤ q₀ ∧
      ∀ x : Fin k → V,
        φ.Realize (Sum.elim x Subtype.val) ↔
          (∀ i, x i ∈ B) ∧ @Structure.RelMap _ V H.structure k R x

/-- The sequence `s` is radius-`r` definable in the graph `G` with `c`
unary predicates, `s'` parameters and quantifier rank `q₀`: for every
step `t` and vertex `v`, the induced partial graph
`s[t][Ball^{s[t+1]}_r(v)]` is definable in some expansion of `G` by `c`
unary predicates, by formulas of quantifier rank at most `q₀` with at
most `s'` parameters. -/
def IsRadiusDefinable (G : SimpleGraph V) (s : List (PartialGraph V))
    (r c s' q₀ : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ (t : ℕ) (ht : t + 1 < s.length) (v : V),
    ∃ (colors : Fin c → Set V) (S : Finset V), S.card ≤ s' ∧
      @DefinableIn V (withColors Language.graph c) (expansion G colors) q₀ S
        s[t] (s[t + 1].ball r v)

end Lax185574.LocalDefinability

concepts.title: Local formulas and basic local sentences
concepts.description:
Fix a finite relational signature σ of arity α. Two σ-formulas φ(x̄)
and ψ(x̄) are *equivalent* if for every σ-structure A and every tuple
ā ∈ V(A)^{|x̄|}, A ⊨ φ(ā) if and only if A ⊨ ψ(ā).

The formula adj_σ(x₁, x₂) tests whether x₁ and x₂ are adjacent in the
Gaifman graph. For every relation R ∈ σ of arity β ≤ α it tests whether
there are elements x₃, …, x_β such that some permutation of x₁, …, x_β
satisfies R. Its quantifier rank is at most α − 2. From it one derives
the formula dist(x₁, x₂) ≤ r, which checks whether x₁ and x₂ have
distance at most r in the Gaifman graph. It quantifies the candidate
vertices of a path and checks the required adjacencies in parallel, so
its quantifier rank is at most r + α.

A σ-formula φ(x̄) is *r-local* if every quantifier appearing in φ(x̄) is
of the form ∀y ∈ Ball_s(x̄) or ∃y ∈ Ball_s(x̄) for some s ≤ r, where the
ball checks are implemented using the dist formulas, which are exempt
from this condition. A sentence ψ is *basic r-local* if there is some
r' ≤ r such that ψ is of the form

  ∃x₁, …, x_m ( ⋀_{1 ≤ i < j ≤ m} dist(xᵢ, xⱼ) > 2r' ∧ ⋀_{1 ≤ i ≤ m} φ(xᵢ) )

for an r'-local formula φ.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
Formulas are mathlib's, `L.Formula (Fin k)` for formulas with free
variables x₁, …, x_k, and `L.BoundedFormula (Fin k) n` for their
subformulas with n further bound variables. A finite relational
signature is a relational language with finitely many relation symbols
in total. The arity bound α plays no role in the definitions.

Equivalence quantifies over all structures whose domain lies in one
universe, which is an explicit parameter of the definition. The domains
may be empty or infinite.

adj_σ is the conjunction of x₁ ≠ x₂ with the disjunction, over the
relation symbols R of arity β ≥ 2, of ∃x₃ … ∃x_β ⋁_π R(x_{π(1)}, …,
x_{π(β)}), where π ranges over the permutations of the β positions. The
quantified variables may coincide with x₁, x₂ or each other, so this is
exactly adjacency in the Gaifman graph. Symbols of arity at most one
contribute nothing. Its quantifier rank is at most α − 2.

dist(x₁, x₂) ≤ r quantifies the r vertices v₁, …, v_r of a walk
x₁ = v₀, v₁, …, v_r, requires v_r = x₂, and requires every step to be
an equality or an adjacency. So it holds exactly if a walk of length at
most r joins x₁ and x₂, as in `GaifmanGraph.WithinDist`. Its quantifier
rank is at most r plus that of adj_σ, so at most r + α. For r = 0 it is
equivalent to the equality x₁ = x₂.

Finite disjunctions and conjunctions are mathlib's `iSup` and `iInf`.
They fix some order of the members, which affects neither the meaning
nor the quantifier rank. A formula over the variables x₁, x₂ is placed
at given terms by substitution.

The guard of a quantifier over Ball_s(x̄) is the disjunction over i of
dist(xᵢ, y) ≤ s, where y is the newly bound variable. For a formula
without free variables, the ball is empty and the guard is falsum. A
local formula is built from atoms by falsum and implication, which give
all Boolean connectives, and by the guarded quantifiers
∀y (guard → φ) and ∃y (guard ∧ φ). The inner formulas of a local
formula may have more free variables than x̄, namely the bound
variables, but the balls are always taken around x̄. The dist formulas
inside the guards are exempt, exactly as in the paper.

In a basic local sentence the m witnesses are the m bound variables of
an existential block, and "dist(xᵢ, xⱼ) > 2r'" is the negation of the
dist formula of radius 2r'. The case m = 0 is allowed and gives a true
sentence.

namespace Lax185574.LocalFormulas

open FirstOrder FirstOrder.Language

universe u v w a

variable {L : Language.{u, v}}

/-- Two formulas are *equivalent* if they hold of the same tuples in
every structure whose domain lies in the universe `w`. -/
def Equivalent {α : Type a} (φ ψ : L.Formula α) : Prop :=
  ∀ (M : Type w) [L.Structure M] (x : α → M), φ.Realize x ↔ ψ.Realize x

/-- Two formulas are *equivalent on finite structures* if they hold of
the same tuples in every finite structure whose domain lies in the
universe `w`. -/
def FinitelyEquivalent {α : Type a} (φ ψ : L.Formula α) : Prop :=
  ∀ (M : Type w) [Finite M] [L.Structure M] (x : α → M), φ.Realize x ↔ ψ.Realize x

/-- The formula `φ(x₁, …, x_j)` with each `xᵢ` replaced by the term
`t i`, as a subformula with `n` bound variables in scope. -/
def instantiate {β : Type*} {j n : ℕ} (φ : L.Formula (Fin j))
    (t : Fin j → L.Term (β ⊕ Fin n)) : L.BoundedFormula β n :=
  (φ.subst t).relabel id

/-- The variable term in position `m` of a relation atom in `adj_σ`:
positions `0` and `1` are `x₁` and `x₂`, and position `m ≥ 2` is the
bound variable `x_{m+1}`. -/
def adjSlot {l : ℕ} (m : Fin l) : L.Term (Fin 2 ⊕ Fin (l - 2)) :=
  if h : m.val < 2 then Term.var (Sum.inl ⟨m.val, h⟩)
  else Term.var (Sum.inr ⟨m.val - 2, by omega⟩)

/-- The part of `adj_σ` for one relation symbol `R` of arity `l`:
`∃x₃ … ∃x_l ⋁_π R(x_{π(1)}, …, x_{π(l)})` if `l ≥ 2`, and falsum
otherwise. -/
noncomputable def adjVia {l : ℕ} (R : L.Relations l) : L.Formula (Fin 2) :=
  if 2 ≤ l then
    BoundedFormula.exs
      (BoundedFormula.iSup fun π : Equiv.Perm (Fin l) =>
        BoundedFormula.rel R fun m => adjSlot (π m))
  else ⊥

variable (L) in
/-- `adj_σ(x₁, x₂)`: the formula stating that `x₁` and `x₂` are adjacent
in the Gaifman graph. -/
noncomputable def adjFormula [Finite (Σ l, L.Relations l)] : L.Formula (Fin 2) :=
  ∼((Term.var (Sum.inl 0)).bdEqual (Term.var (Sum.inl 1))) ⊓
    BoundedFormula.iSup fun R : Σ l, L.Relations l => adjVia R.2

/-- The vertex `v_i` of the walk quantified in `dist(x₁, x₂) ≤ r`:
`v₀ = x₁`, and `v_i` for `i ≥ 1` is the `i`-th bound variable. -/
def walkVertex {r : ℕ} (i : Fin (r + 1)) : L.Term (Fin 2 ⊕ Fin r) :=
  Fin.cases (motive := fun _ => L.Term (Fin 2 ⊕ Fin r))
    (Term.var (Sum.inl 0)) (fun j => Term.var (Sum.inr j)) i

variable (L) in
/-- `dist(x₁, x₂) ≤ r`: there are `v₁, …, v_r` with `v_r = x₂` such that
each step of `x₁ = v₀, v₁, …, v_r` is an equality or an adjacency. -/
noncomputable def distFormula [Finite (Σ l, L.Relations l)] (r : ℕ) :
    L.Formula (Fin 2) :=
  BoundedFormula.exs
    (((walkVertex (L := L) (Fin.last r)).bdEqual (Term.var (Sum.inl 1))) ⊓
      BoundedFormula.iInf fun i : Fin r =>
        ((walkVertex (L := L) i.castSucc).bdEqual (walkVertex i.succ)) ⊔
          instantiate (adjFormula L) ![walkVertex i.castSucc, walkVertex i.succ])

variable (L) in
/-- The guard `y ∈ Ball_s(x̄)` of a local quantifier, where `x̄` are the
`k` free variables and `y` is the newly bound variable: the disjunction
over `i` of `dist(xᵢ, y) ≤ s`. -/
noncomputable def ballGuard [Finite (Σ l, L.Relations l)] (k s n : ℕ) :
    L.BoundedFormula (Fin k) (n + 1) :=
  BoundedFormula.iSup fun i : Fin k =>
    instantiate (distFormula L s) ![Term.var (Sum.inl i), Term.var (Sum.inr (Fin.last n))]

/-- `IsLocal r φ`: the formula `φ` with free variables `x̄ = x₁, …, x_k`
and `n` further bound variables in scope is `r`-local. It is built from
atoms by falsum, implication and quantifiers guarded by `Ball_s(x̄)` for
some `s ≤ r`. -/
inductive IsLocal [Finite (Σ l, L.Relations l)] (r : ℕ) {k : ℕ} :
    {n : ℕ} → L.BoundedFormula (Fin k) n → Prop
  /-- Falsum is local. -/
  | falsum {n : ℕ} : IsLocal r (BoundedFormula.falsum : L.BoundedFormula (Fin k) n)
  /-- Equality atoms are local. -/
  | equal {n : ℕ} (t₁ t₂ : L.Term (Fin k ⊕ Fin n)) :
      IsLocal r (BoundedFormula.equal t₁ t₂)
  /-- Relation atoms are local. -/
  | rel {n l : ℕ} (R : L.Relations l) (ts : Fin l → L.Term (Fin k ⊕ Fin n)) :
      IsLocal r (BoundedFormula.rel R ts)
  /-- Implications of local formulas are local. -/
  | imp {n : ℕ} {φ ψ : L.BoundedFormula (Fin k) n} :
      IsLocal r φ → IsLocal r ψ → IsLocal r (φ.imp ψ)
  /-- `∀y ∈ Ball_s(x̄) φ`, that is `∀y (y ∈ Ball_s(x̄) → φ)`, for `s ≤ r`. -/
  | all {n s : ℕ} {φ : L.BoundedFormula (Fin k) (n + 1)} :
      s ≤ r → IsLocal r φ → IsLocal r (∀' (ballGuard L k s n ⟹ φ))
  /-- `∃y ∈ Ball_s(x̄) φ`, that is `∃y (y ∈ Ball_s(x̄) ∧ φ)`, for `s ≤ r`. -/
  | ex {n s : ℕ} {φ : L.BoundedFormula (Fin k) (n + 1)} :
      s ≤ r → IsLocal r φ → IsLocal r (∃' (ballGuard L k s n ⊓ φ))

variable (L) in
/-- The sentence `∃x₁, …, x_m (⋀_{i < j} dist(xᵢ, xⱼ) > 2r' ∧ ⋀_i φ(xᵢ))`. -/
noncomputable def basicLocalSentence [Finite (Σ l, L.Relations l)] (r' m : ℕ)
    (φ : L.Formula (Fin 1)) : L.Sentence :=
  BoundedFormula.exs
    ((BoundedFormula.iInf fun p : {p : Fin m × Fin m // p.1 < p.2} =>
        ∼(instantiate (distFormula L (2 * r'))
          ![Term.var (Sum.inr p.1.1), Term.var (Sum.inr p.1.2)])) ⊓
      BoundedFormula.iInf fun i : Fin m => instantiate φ ![Term.var (Sum.inr i)])

/-- `IsBasicLocal r ψ`: the sentence `ψ` is basic `r`-local. -/
def IsBasicLocal [Finite (Σ l, L.Relations l)] (r : ℕ) (ψ : L.Sentence) : Prop :=
  ∃ r' ≤ r, ∃ (m : ℕ) (φ : L.Formula (Fin 1)),
    IsLocal r' φ ∧ ψ = basicLocalSentence L r' m φ

end Lax185574.LocalFormulas

concepts.title: Local formulas are evaluated in any superset of the ball
concepts.description:
Let φ(x̄) be an r-local σ-formula, let A be a σ-structure, let
ā ∈ V(A)^{|x̄|}, and let Ball^A_r(ā) ⊆ B ⊆ V(A). Then
A ⊨ φ(ā) if and only if A[B] ⊨ φ(ā).

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The signature is a finite relational language, as required by the
definition of local formulas. The structure is arbitrary, possibly
infinite. The tuple is given as a tuple of B, and its image in A is its
coordinatewise image. The formula is evaluated in A[B] with the induced
structure of `GaifmanGraph.induced`, whose Gaifman graph may have fewer
edges than the restriction of the Gaifman graph of A to B.

concepts.title: Types are determined by types in a neighborhood
concepts.description:
For all k, q, α ∈ ℕ there is a number q' = q'(k, q, α) such that with
h ≔ 7^q the following holds. Let σ be a relational signature of arity at most
α and A a σ-structure. Then, for all ā ∈ V(A)^k and B ⊇ Ball^A_h(ā),
the type tp^A_q(ā) depends only on tp^{A[B]}_{q'}(ā).

This is a corollary of Gaifman's locality theorem. The point is that h
depends on q alone, and q' does not depend on the signature beyond its
arity. The latter matters when the signature has one unary symbol per
part of a partition with up to n parts. The paper states that h = h(q)
is computable, and its proof takes h = 7^q. The statement here names
this value, because algorithms downstream compute the radius from q.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
"Depends only on" is stated pairwise. If ā with B ⊇ Ball_h(ā) and b̄ with
B' ⊇ Ball_h(b̄) have the same type of rank q' in A[B] and A[B']
respectively, then they have the same type of rank q in A. The tuples
are given as tuples of B and B', and their images in A are their
coordinates. Types without parameters are compared as sets of formulas
of one fixed language, so types in different substructures are
comparable.

The paper states the lemma for finite signatures, with h and q'
computable. Here the signature is any relational language with relation
symbols of arity at most α, possibly infinitely many. This is the
generality that the lemma is applied in, as the language of partial
graphs has a unary symbol for every natural number. For an infinite
signature the statement follows from the finite case, applied to the
finitely many symbols of each formula, since q' does not depend on the
signature. The structure is finite. The radius is h = 7^q. The rank q' only exists, as no algorithm
uses it.
