import Lax199508.NeighborhoodComplexity
import Mathlib.Data.ENat.Lattice

/-!
---
title: Neighborhood complexity and VC-dimension
type: definition
---
The *neighborhood complexity* of a graph G is the function π_G : ℕ → ℕ
defined by

π_G(k) ≔ max_{S ⊆ V(G), |S| ≤ k} |{ N^G(v) ∩ S : v ∈ V(G) }|,

which counts the maximum number of distinct neighborhoods of vertices of
G restricted to a set of size at most k.

The *VC-dimension* of a graph G is the maximal size of a set A ⊆ V(G)
such that { N(v) ∩ A : v ∈ V(G) } = 2^A.

# Formalization notes

The number of traces |{ N^G(v) ∩ S : v ∈ V(G) }| is `traceCount` of the
Sparsity Lectures submission (Lax199508), which is the cardinality of
the set of traces. For a finite set S the traces are subsets of S, so
there are at most 2^|S| of them and the count is exact. The maximum over
all S with |S| ≤ k is the supremum of a set of natural numbers bounded
by 2^k, so it is attained.

A set A is shattered if every subset B ⊆ A is the trace N(v) ∩ A of some
vertex v. The VC-dimension is the supremum of the sizes of the finite
shattered sets, an extended natural number. It is the maximum of the
paper whenever that exists, and ⊤ for a graph with arbitrarily large
shattered sets. "VC-dimension at most d" is `vcDim G ≤ d`.
-/

namespace Lax185574.VCDimension

open Lax199508.NeighborhoodComplexity

universe u

variable {V : Type u}

/-- The neighborhood complexity `π_G(k)`: the largest number of
neighborhood traces `N(v) ∩ S` on a set `S` of at most `k` vertices. -/
noncomputable def neighborhoodComplexity (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sSup {m | ∃ S : Finset V, S.card ≤ k ∧ m = traceCount G (S : Set V)}

/-- The neighborhoods of `G` shatter `A`: every subset of `A` is the
trace `N(v) ∩ A` of some vertex `v`. -/
def Shatters (G : SimpleGraph V) (A : Finset V) : Prop :=
  ∀ B ⊆ A, ∃ v : V, ∀ a ∈ A, (G.Adj v a ↔ a ∈ B)

/-- The VC-dimension of `G`: the supremum of the sizes of the finite
vertex sets shattered by the neighborhoods. -/
noncomputable def vcDim (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ∞ :=
  ⨆ (A : Finset V) (_ : Shatters G A), (A.card : ℕ∞)

end Lax185574.VCDimension

concepts.title: Bounded-VC duality
concepts.description:
For a graph G and sets S, X ⊆ V(G), the set S *dominates* X if every
vertex of X ∖ S has a neighbor in S, and S *antidominates* X if every
vertex of X ∖ S has a nonneighbor in S.

For every d ∈ ℕ there is some k ∈ ℕ with the following property. Let G
be a graph of VC-dimension at most d, and let X, Y ⊆ V(G) be two
(possibly overlapping) sets with at least one of X, Y finite. Then there
exists a set sample(X, Y) of size at most k such that at least one of
the following holds:

1. sample(X, Y) is contained in Y and dominates X,
2. sample(X, Y) is contained in X and antidominates Y.

This is a corollary of the (p, q)-theorem for bounded VC-dimension.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The graph is finite, so the hypothesis that X or Y is finite always
holds and is omitted. The paper also allows infinite graphs. Every
application in the paper, through the ball-flip lemma inside the proof
of the closure theorem, is to a finite graph. The bound k is chosen
before the graph. VC-dimension is `VCDimension.vcDim`.

concepts.sourceText:
import Lax185574.VCDimension

/-!
---
title: Bounded-VC duality
type: lemma
---
For a graph G and sets S, X ⊆ V(G), the set S *dominates* X if every
vertex of X ∖ S has a neighbor in S, and S *antidominates* X if every
vertex of X ∖ S has a nonneighbor in S.

For every d ∈ ℕ there is some k ∈ ℕ with the following property. Let G
be a graph of VC-dimension at most d, and let X, Y ⊆ V(G) be two
(possibly overlapping) sets with at least one of X, Y finite. Then there
exists a set sample(X, Y) of size at most k such that at least one of
the following holds:

1. sample(X, Y) is contained in Y and dominates X,
2. sample(X, Y) is contained in X and antidominates Y.

This is a corollary of the (p, q)-theorem for bounded VC-dimension.

# Formalization notes

The graph is finite, so the hypothesis that X or Y is finite always
holds and is omitted. The paper also allows infinite graphs. Every
application in the paper, through the ball-flip lemma inside the proof
of the closure theorem, is to a finite graph. The bound k is chosen
before the graph. VC-dimension is `VCDimension.vcDim`.
-/

namespace Lax185574.VCDuality

open Lax185574.VCDimension

universe u

variable {V : Type u}

/-- `S` dominates `X` in `G`: every vertex of `X ∖ S` has a neighbor in
`S`. -/
def Dominates (G : SimpleGraph V) (S X : Set V) : Prop :=
  ∀ x ∈ X \ S, ∃ y ∈ S, G.Adj x y

/-- `S` antidominates `X` in `G`: every vertex of `X ∖ S` has a
nonneighbor in `S`. -/
def Antidominates (G : SimpleGraph V) (S X : Set V) : Prop :=
  ∀ x ∈ X \ S, ∃ y ∈ S, ¬ G.Adj x y

/-- **Bounded-VC duality.** In a finite graph of VC-dimension at most
`d`, for any two vertex sets `X` and `Y`, some set of at most `k(d)`
vertices of `Y` dominates `X`, or some set of at most `k(d)` vertices of
`X` antidominates `Y`. -/
axiom vc_duality (d : ℕ) :
    ∃ k : ℕ, ∀ (V : Type u) [Finite V] (G : SimpleGraph V), vcDim G ≤ d →
      ∀ X Y : Set V, ∃ S : Finset V, S.card ≤ k ∧
        (((S : Set V) ⊆ Y ∧ Dominates G S X) ∨
          ((S : Set V) ⊆ X ∧ Antidominates G S Y))

end Lax185574.VCDuality

  Exists fun k =>
    ∀ (V : Type u) [Finite V] (G : SimpleGraph V),
      instLEENat.le (Lax185574.VCDimension.vcDim G) d.cast →
        ∀ (X Y : Set V),
          Exists fun S =>
            And (instLENat.le S.card k)
              (Or
                (And (Set.instLE.le (Finset.instSetLike.coe S) Y)
                  (Lax185574.VCDuality.Dominates G (Finset.instSetLike.coe S) X))
                (And (Set.instLE.le (Finset.instSetLike.coe S) X)
                  (Lax185574.VCDuality.Antidominates G (Finset.instSetLike.coe S) Y)))

concepts.title: Radius-r depth-q width of a construction sequence
concepts.description:
For r, q ∈ ℕ, the *radius-r depth-q width* of a construction sequence
G₁, …, G_λ is

max_{t ∈ [λ−1]} max_{v ∈ V(G)} |Types^{G_t}_{q,q}(Ball^{G_{t+1}}_r(v))|.

It measures a construction sequence by the number of types of q-tuples
realized near each vertex. Types are taken in G_t, and balls in G_{t+1}.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The partial graph `G_t` is the relational structure of
`Lax185574.PartialGraphs`, with edges, non-edges and one unary relation
per color. The types are those of `Lax185574.FirstOrderTypes`, without
parameters, `typeCount`. The maximum is the supremum of a set of natural numbers.
That set is finite when the vertex type is finite, which is the case in
every statement that uses the width. The empty maximum, for a sequence
of length one, is 0.

import Lax185574.ConstructionSequences
import Lax185574.FirstOrderTypes
import Mathlib.Order.ConditionallyCompleteLattice.Basic
import Mathlib.Data.Nat.Lattice

/-!
---
title: Radius-r depth-q width of a construction sequence
type: definition
---
For r, q ∈ ℕ, the *radius-r depth-q width* of a construction sequence
G₁, …, G_λ is

max_{t ∈ [λ−1]} max_{v ∈ V(G)} |Types^{G_t}_{q,q}(Ball^{G_{t+1}}_r(v))|.

It measures a construction sequence by the number of types of q-tuples
realized near each vertex. Types are taken in G_t, and balls in G_{t+1}.

# Formalization notes

The partial graph `G_t` is the relational structure of
`Lax185574.PartialGraphs`, with edges, non-edges and one unary relation
per color. The types are those of `Lax185574.FirstOrderTypes`, without
parameters, `typeCount`. The maximum is the supremum of a set of natural numbers.
That set is finite when the vertex type is finite, which is the case in
every statement that uses the width. The empty maximum, for a sequence
of length one, is 0.
-/

namespace Lax185574.Width

open Lax185574.PartialGraphs Lax185574.FirstOrderTypes

universe z

variable {V : Type z}

/-- The number of types of `q`-tuples of quantifier rank `q`, in the
partial graph `G`, realized by tuples from the set `X`. -/
noncomputable def partialTypeCount (G : PartialGraph V) (k q : ℕ) (X : Set V) : ℕ :=
  @typeCount language V G.structure k q X

/-- The radius-`r` depth-`q` width of the sequence `s`: the largest
number of types of `q`-tuples of quantifier rank `q` in `s[t]` realized
by tuples from a ball of radius `r` in `s[t+1]`. -/
noncomputable def width (r q : ℕ) (s : List (PartialGraph V)) : ℕ :=
  sSup {K | ∃ (t : ℕ) (ht : t + 1 < s.length) (v : V),
    K = partialTypeCount s[t] q q (s[t + 1].ball r v)}

end Lax185574.Width

proofs.description:
The proof in the paper. Group `A` by neighborhoods in the ball `B` and
`B` by neighborhoods in `A`. The parameter set consists of
representatives of all groups and of a bounded-VC duality sample for
every pair of groups of `A` and for every group of `B` against the inner
ball. The `S`-flip toggles exactly the pairs of atomic types joined by
an edge of `G` between `A` and `B`. Then `A` and `B` are non-adjacent in
the flip, the inner ball is unchanged, and it has no edges to the
outside of `B`, so the ball of radius `r + 1` still avoids `A`. The
duality is used in a form without exception for the sample, obtained
from the concept at the cost of doubling the sample.

The proof in the paper. For each symmetric `R ⊆ Π^s × Π^s` let `φ_R(z̄
x, y)` express distance at most `r` in `G ⊕ (z̄, R)`, using the
quantifier-free edge formula of the flip. Let `k` exceed all the bounds
on `φ_R`-patterns and put `t = Q(k · 9^s)`. For every `R`, every `N ∈
{E, ¬E}` and every base `b̄ ∈ A^k` fix a `(φ_R, N)`-pattern of maximum
height (less than `k`), and let `A*` consist of `A` and all their grid
points. If a ball `B = Ball^H_r[v]` in `H = G ⊕ (p̄, R)` avoids `A*` but
realizes more than `t` atomic types over `A`, the matching theorem gives
atomically matched tuples in `B` and `A` of length `k · 9^s`. By
pigeonhole `k` of the pairs have the same pair of atomic types over
`p̄`, so on them `H` agrees with `G` or with its complement, and this
yields `N` such that the tuple `w̄` from `A` and the tuple `ū` from `B`
satisfy `N(wⱼ, uⱼ)` and `¬N(wⱼ', uⱼ)` for `j < j'`. Then `p̄ v` and `ū`
extend the chosen pattern with base `w̄` by a row, as `ū` lies in `B`
and the old grid points do not, contradicting maximality.

The argument is carried out for the graph classes of the archive and
their monadic dependence, and transferred to the graph classes used
here.

The statement for graphs and `Algorithm.Computes`, from
the version for simple graphs: the algorithm is the program with
its exponent, the merge sequence of a graph is that of its simple graph,
and the constant stays the same.

Flip a cell of the four-part partition exactly when it contains an
edge `uv` of `B` with no walk of length at most `6` in `B̄`. Then every
edge of `B'` that is an edge of `B` has a short walk in `B̄`, by the
choice of the flipped cells. Every edge of `B'` that is a non-edge of
`B` lies in a flipped cell, and comparing it with the edge that caused
the flip gives a walk of length at most `6` in `B` between its ends, by
a case analysis over the adjacencies to the representatives. Walks
between the two sides of a bipartite graph have odd length, so the
bound `6` improves to `5`.

The construction is adapted from an earlier formalization that proves
the statement with bound `6` for flips given by Boolean toggles, see
PROVENANCE.md.

Concatenate the two tuples to one tuple of length `2ℓ` and apply the
Erdős–Rado theorem for order types of tuples to the induced coloring.
This gives a set `H` of size `2m` on which the color depends only on the
order type of the concatenation. Split `H` into its `m` smallest
elements `I` and its `m` largest elements `J`. Every entry from `I` lies
below every entry from `J`, so for `a ∈ I^ℓ` and `b ∈ J^ℓ` the order
type of the concatenation is determined by the order types of `a` and
`b`. The function `U(t)` is the largest `m ≤ t` such that every `n ≥ t`
admits such sets of size `m` for every coloring. It is non-decreasing by
definition and unbounded by the Ramsey step.

The Ramsey core is adapted from lax-345067 (finite Ramsey theorems for

A monadically dependent class has bounded VC-dimension, since otherwise
the edge formula has the independence property on it.

The program reads the list of words into arrays, the entries one after
the other with the start and the length of every word. It then selects
the distinct words in increasing order: in round `t` it scans all words
and keeps the smallest one above the word selected in round `t - 1`,
comparing words lexicographically entry by entry. The indices of the
selected words are recorded, and finally their number and their frames
are written. With `m` words of total length `N`, this takes
`O(m² · N)` steps, so cubic time in the length of the input. Every value
the program produces is at most the length of the input plus its
largest entry, so word-length exponent `1` suffices.

Induction on `r`, as in the paper. At radius 0 take `A* = A` and no
flip. For the step, enlarge `A` to `A₁` by the ball-types lemma for the
current parameter bound `s`, and apply the induction hypothesis to `A₁`,
giving `B`. The `s`-definable flips of graphs of the class form a
monadically dependent class, so they have VC-dimension at most some `d`.
For every set `S ⊆ B` of at most `s` vertices and every `S`-flip `H` (at
most `2^{9^s}` of them), group the vertices whose radius-`r` ball in `H`
avoids `A₁` by the set of atomic types over `A` that the ball meets. By
the ball-types lemma these profiles have at most `t` members, and by the
Sauer–Shelah lemma there are at most `|A| + (|A| + 1)^d` atomic types
over `A`, so there are polynomially many groups. The ball flip lemma
gives a `z`-definable flip of `H` that `(r + 1)`-separates each group
from `A`, which is an `(s + z)`-definable flip of `G` by transitivity.
The new closure is `A₁` together with the parameters of all these flips.
Vertices of `A₁ ∖ A` are isolated by the flip over themselves.

Apply the closure theorem at radius `6r` to obtain `A*` and the sets
`S(v)`. For every `T ⊆ A*` of size at most `k·s₀`, the partition-metric
conversion applied to `𝒫_T`, which has at most `3^{k s₀}` parts, gives one
flip `H_T` whose radius-`r` balls lie in the radius-`6r` balls of the
flip metric of `𝒫_T`. For a tuple `v̄` outside `A` take
`T = S(v₁) ∪ … ∪ S(v_k)`. As `𝒫_T` refines `𝒫_{S(vᵢ)}`, the flip metric
of `𝒫_T` dominates that of `𝒫_{S(vᵢ)}`, and the latter is at least the
distance in the `S(vᵢ)`-flip from the closure theorem, which exceeds `6r`.
So `H_T` separates `v̄` from `A` at distance more than `r`. There are at
most `(|A*| + 1)^{k s₀}` sets `T`.

The existence of an admissible pair is the grouping iteration: start with
all indices surviving at scale `r`, and while two surviving entries are
within eight times the scale, drop one of them and multiply the scale by
nine. At the end, entries of one group are within twice the scale `ρ`,
hence within `4ρ − 2r`, and entries of different groups are farther apart
than `6ρ ≥ 4ρ + 2r`.

For the detection property, if every vertex of `X` is near the tuple,
then the vertices of `S` lie in distinct blocks, by the scattering of `S`.
Conversely, if some vertex `x₀` of `X` is far from the tuple and no vertex
of `X` is at a distance between `r` and `H`, then the blocks met by `X`
inject into `S` minus the representative of `x₀`.

If some two vertices `u`, `v` are not joined by a walk of length at
most `2` in `G`, then they are distinct, non-adjacent and have no common
neighbor. In `Ḡ` they are adjacent, and every other vertex is adjacent to
`u` or to `v`. So any two vertices are joined in `Ḡ` by a walk that goes
to `u` or `v`, possibly crosses the edge `uv`, and leaves again, of
length at most `3`.

The program runs the glue program `StpRam.glue` and the program of the
rank shift lemma in the loop driver `loop_sound`, as in the proof of the lemma on computing scatter types. The first round
reads the graph, `k` and `q`, skips the distance matrix `D_G` and reads
the family of type trees. For `q = 0` it outputs the empty scatter type.
Otherwise the rounds ask for the shifts of the entries of the list of
the family trees followed by the answers, one by one, so that the
answers are the trees `tree_{k+i,q−i}(v)` for `1 ≤ i ≤ q` and all
vertices `v`, in this order. After a dummy call the final round reads
the graph, `D_G` and the answers and computes the scatter type
(`StpRam.finalRound_run`). Its greedy scans test whether a vertex is
within distance `r` of a chosen vertex by one entry of the row of `D_G`
of the chosen vertex, in place of a breadth-first search. The script has
`q · n + 1` calls. Every run inside the driver is right at an admissible
word length: the runs of the glue program because their values are below
a constant in `k, q` times the cube of `|x| + max x + 1`, the runs of
the rank shift because their queries are admissible at the word lengths
of their regions. The time is that of the first round, `O_{k,q}(n² + n ·
L)`, and of the final round, `O_{k,q}(n² · (L + 1))`, plus `q · n`
middle rounds of time `O_{k,q}(n · L)` and `q · n + 1` calls of time
`O_{k,q}((L + 1)^a)`.

Two threads run in parallel at a word length a constant below the given
one. The first thread removes the graph from the input and runs a loop
that alternates a glue program with a callee. The glue program follows
the construction sequence step by step. It keeps the current partial
graph with its matrix of distances and the type trees of all vertices,
and issues one call per step and finally one call of the evaluation on
the tree of a vertex and the localized sentence. For a merge step the
callee maps the merge lift over the trees of all vertices, for a resolve
step it runs the resolve lift, which also returns the new matrix of
distances. Each query is guarded for the word length of its callee, so
every halting run of the pipeline is right, and the pipeline halts
within `c · m · (n + 1)² · (K + 1) ^ b` steps when the input is long
enough. The
second thread evaluates the sentence by brute force, which is fast for
short inputs and for graphs without vertices. The combinator outputs the
answer of a thread that halts.

The proof is carried out for the input format with the graph in

Two distinct vertices are adjacent in `G ⊕ (p̄, R)` exactly when either
they are adjacent and the pair of their atomic types over `p̄` is not in
`R`, or they are non-adjacent and the pair is in `R`. Membership of the
pair of atomic types in `R` is a finite disjunction, over the pairs in
`R`, of conjunctions of the atomic formulas `x = pᵢ`, `x ≠ pᵢ ∧ E(x, pᵢ)`
and `x ≠ pᵢ ∧ ¬E(x, pᵢ)`.

Let `S₁` and `S₂` witness the two flips and put `S = S₁ ∪ S₂`. The
partition into atomic types over `S` in `G₀` refines the one over `S₁`
in `G₀`, and also the one over `S₂` in `G₁`: two vertices outside `S`
with the same neighbors in `S` lie in the same part over `S₁`, so their
adjacency to a vertex of `S₂` is preserved or complemented alike when
passing to `G₁`. A flip of a flip is a flip for a common refinement.

The proof of the theorem on definable construction sequences. Compute a
chain at radius `5r + 1` and accuracy `ε` (the chain theorem), of length
`m ≤ O(r/ε)`, and turn it into a construction sequence (the lemma
turning chains into construction sequences). With `k_r ≤ c (n+1)^ε` the
radius-`(5r+1)` width of the chain, `d` a bound on the VC-dimension of
the graphs of the class (the observation on bounded VC-dimension) and
`π_G(k) ≤ (k+1)^d` (the Sauer–Shelah lemma), `w_r ≤ (k_r + 1)^(d+1)`, so
`a₀ = d + 1`. The length is `O(n w₁) ≤ O(n w_r)`, as the width of a
chain grows with the radius. The number of predicates is `2m + 1 ≤ ⌈A
r/ε⌉ + A`. On the word RAM, a first phase converts the compressed sparse
row form of the graph into the word of the graph that the two cited
programs read.

Let `q'` be the rank of `LocalToGlobal` for `q`-tuples, rank `q` and arity
2, and let `a` and `F` be the exponent and factor of `TypeBound` for
`q`-tuples and rank `q' + q₀`. Fix a step `t` and a vertex `v`, and let
`B` and `W` be the balls of radius `r` and `r + 7^q` around `v` in the
next partial graph. A step keeps resolved pairs, so the radius-`7^q` ball
in the current partial graph of a tuple from `B` lies in `W`. By
`LocalToGlobal`, the type of such a tuple is determined by its type of
rank `q'` in the induced partial graph on `W`. This partial graph is
definable in an expansion of the graph by `c` predicates with at most `s`
parameters, so the type over the parameters of rank `q' + q₀` determines
the latter. `TypeBound` bounds the number of these types by
`F · (s + 1)^a`.

The program reads the tree, copies the word of its root into an array,
reads the code of the formula into a second array, and lists the nodes
of the tree in breadth-first order. It fills a table with a row for
every position of the code and a column for every node, from the last
position to the first. At a position where a subformula starts, the
entry of a node is the value of the subformula at the node: an atom is
looked up among the atom codes of the node, a negation or a conjunction
is read off the rows of its subformulas, and `∃ y (dist(xᵢ, y) ≤ s ∧ ψ)`
holds if some extension of the node with guard `i` has a child where `ψ`
holds, read off the row of `ψ`. A second table records where every
subformula ends, which locates the second conjunct of a conjunction.
This is the recursion of the proof of the evaluation lemma over pairs of
a subformula and a node. The answer is the entry of the first position
at the root, which is the semantic core `evalNode`, whose correctness is
`evalNode_node`. A cell takes time linear in the length of the input, so
the time is a polynomial of degree three. Every value is at most a
constant times the square of the input length, so word-length exponent
`2` suffices.

The program runs a glue program and the three programs of the
restriction lemma, the rank shift lemma and the canonical form
observation in the loop driver. The glue program runs the recursion of
the far composition with an explicit stack of frames: each round reads
the stack and the answer to its last question, does one step of the
recursion and asks the next question, a rank shift, a restriction or a
canonical form, or writes the type tree of the concatenation. Before it
halts, every round checks that the question is admissible for the
program that answers it, that the round counter is small against the
word length of its region, and that its output fits, so every halting
run inside the driver is right.

The proof of the few-types theorem. Run the algorithm of the theorem on
definable construction sequences with radius `r + 7^q`, where `h = 7^q`
is the radius of the lemma passing from definability to few types. The
output is radius-`(r + 7^q)` definable with `⌈A(r + 7^q)/ε⌉ + A`
predicates and `s ≤ c₀ (n+1)^(a₀ε)` parameters, so its radius-`r`
depth-`q` width is at most `F (s+1)^D`, which is `O((n+1)^(a₀Dε))`. So
`a = a₀D + a₀` works for the width and the length, and `a ≥ 1` since `a₀
≥ 1`. The exponent `3 + η` of the time is passed on to the theorem on
definable construction sequences. The program is a simulation of the
program of the theorem on definable construction sequences on the
rewritten input, one word bit shorter, and the word-length exponent
grows by one to pay for the larger first entry.

Every `𝒫`-flip is a `𝒬`-flip, so a bound on the distance in all
`𝒬`-flips is in particular a bound in all `𝒫`-flips.

Each part of `𝒬` lies in a part of `𝒫`, so the choice between agreeing
and disagreeing made for a pair of `𝒫`-parts also serves the pair of
`𝒬`-parts inside it.

A flip for a partition into at most `p` parts is obtained from the
original graph by a fixed transduction: color the parts with `p` unary
predicates and flip the adjacency between the chosen pairs of colors.
This bounded-flip image of a class is transduced by it, and monadic
dependence is preserved under
transductions. Every `s`-definable flip is a flip for the partition into
atomic types over at most `s` vertices, which has at most `3^s` parts.

A `φ`-pattern is a `(φ, E)`-pattern or a `(φ, ¬E)`-pattern. Take the
larger of the two bounds of the lemma on `(φ, ψ)`-patterns, and use that

The proof in the paper. Color a pair of index pairs `((i, i'), (j, j'))`
by the truth values of `φ(āᵢ', c_{i,j})` and `ψ(b̄ⱼ', c_{i,j})`, and
take homogeneous sets `I`, `J` by the bipartite Ramsey lemma. Pair up
consecutive elements of `I` and `J`: with `ūᵢ = āᵣ āᵣ'` for the `2i`-th
and `(2i+1)`-st elements `r < r'` of `I`, likewise `w̄ⱼ`, and `d_{i,j} =
c_{r,s}`, the exclusive or `φ(x̄₁, z) ⊕ φ(x̄₂, z)` holds of `ūᵢ',
d_{i,j}` exactly when `i' = i`: earlier pairs see two equal truth values
by homogeneity, the pair itself sees true then false, and later pairs
see false twice. The same holds for the columns. Then the formula `γ =
∃z (U(z) ∧ (φ ⊕ φ) ∧ (ψ ⊕ ψ))`, with `U` coloring the grid points `d_{i,
h(J)}` for `i ∈ J`, encodes membership `i ∈ J` for an injection `h` of
the subsets of `[k]` into the columns. By Baldwin–Shelah this bounds
`k`, hence the order of the pattern.

The formula is translated into the syntax of the normal form of lax-512892,
over a vocabulary with one symbol for each relation symbol and a nullary
symbol for falsum. Its normal form has radii at most `7^q − 1` and at most
`q + k` witnesses in each basic local sentence. Every local formula in it
has quantifier depth at most `q · (k + q + 2 + 6 · 7^q + 4α)`, a bound that
depends on the arity `α` of the vocabulary but not on its symbols. Back in
mathlib's syntax, each ball-restricted quantifier gets a dist-formula guard
of quantifier rank at most `7^q + α`, which gives the rank bound
`p = q · (k + q + 2 + 6 · 7^q + 4α) + q + k + 2 · 7^q + 2α`.

As in the paper, for each pair of parts of `𝒬 = 𝒫 ∧ T` we find a flip of
`G` on these parts whose edges lie in `R`. Then the pairs outside `R`
are non-edges of the flip, so they are all edges or all non-edges of
`G`. Two parts of `𝒬` inside one part `X` of `𝒫`: by the diameter lemma,
`G[X]` or `Ḡ[X]` has diameter at most `3`. In the first case every
non-adjacent pair of `X` is joined by a walk of length at most `4`
between opposite copies in `G[X, X]` and by an edge in `Ḡ[X, X]`, so it
lies in `R`, and the second case is symmetric. Parts inside different
parts `X`, `Y` of `𝒫`: apply the bipartite flip lemma to `G[X, Y]` with
the representatives in `T`. The parts of `𝒬` refine the four parts of
that lemma, so the flip is constant on the pair.

If a formula `φ(x, y)` has the independence property on `C`, then for a
graph `H` on `m` vertices take the elements `a₀, …, a_{m-1}` and color
the set `A` of them and the set `B` of the elements `b_{ij}` for the
edges `ij` of `H`. Two distinct elements of `A` are adjacent in `H` if
and only if they have a common `φ`-neighbor in `B`. So `C` transduces
all graphs. Conversely, a transduction of all graphs produces the
incidence graph between `{0, …, m-1}` and its subsets, so its edge
formula has the independence property.

The argument is carried out for the graph classes of the archive and

here and the translation
of formulas.

Suppose `φ(x̄; ȳ)` has the independence property on `C`. The left tuple is
not empty, since otherwise all `aᵢ` agree. By Shelah's reduction, carried
out with Ramsey's theorem on finite shattered sequences, some formula
`ψ(x; z̄)` with a single left variable has the independence property, and
so has its dual `ψ*(z̄; x)`. Then `ψ*(z̄; x) ∧ ψ*(z̄'; x)` codes pairs: for
tuples `aᵢ` and `a_{n+j}` the elements `b_{{k, n+l}}` satisfy it exactly
when `(i, j) = (k, l)`. Among all formulas coding on `C`, with any number
of colors, take one of least total arity. If it has two left variables,
then either `x` extends by elements of a color `A` to a tuple coding `z`
and no other element of a color `C`, which is a coding formula with a
single left variable, or a spurious witness gives a coding formula with
parameters and fewer left variables. By symmetry the minimal formula is
`θ(x, y, z)` in single variables. With a color `C₀` for the codes `c_{i,J}`
with `i ∈ J`, the formula `∃z (C₀(z) ∧ θ(x, y, z))` has the independence
property. So `C` is not monadically dependent.

An `r`-local formula holds of a tuple in a structure if and only if it
holds of the tuple in an induced substructure that contains the ball of
radius `r` around the tuple. The quantifiers of the formula are guarded by
balls of radius at most `r` around the tuple, and these balls are the same
in the structure and in the substructure, since a walk of length at most
`r` from the tuple uses only relation tuples whose entries lie in the ball.

Let `q' = p(α, q, k)` be given by `GaifmanLocality`. A formula of rank at
most `q` uses finitely many relation symbols. Over the sublanguage of these
symbols it is equivalent, on finite structures, to a Boolean combination of
basic `7^q`-local sentences and `7^q`-local formulas of rank at most `q'`.
The sentences have the same truth value for both tuples. A local formula
holds of a tuple in the structure if and only if it holds in the induced
substructure, by `LocalSubstructure`, since the balls of the sublanguage are
contained in those of `L`. In the induced substructures, the two tuples
satisfy the same formulas of rank at most `q'`.

Ding, Oporowski, Oxley and Vertigan, Cor. 2.4, through an explicit Ramsey bound and a staircase argument
on homogeneous matrices. The number of atomic types of the left side
over the right side is the number of distinct neighborhoods. A
half-graph with `i ≤ j` becomes one with `j ≤ i` by reversing both
tuples.

The program is one pass over the tree followed by restoring canonical
form, as in the proof of the merge lift lemma. The pass reads the tree
and the colors `P` and `Q`, lists the nodes of the tree in breadth-first
order, and writes for every node, from the last to the first, its
transformed atoms and its extensions. An atom is transformed by
replacing the color `Q` by `P` in every atom `Y(x)` and `dist(x, Y) <
r`. The guards are kept, and the child of an extension is referred to by
the indices of the jobs of the child. Nothing is sorted in the pass. The
canonical form is then restored from the leaves up by the program of the
canonical form observation, called once for every set of the result
(`TreeCanon.treeCanon`), which merges atoms that become equal. This is
the semantic core `mergeNode`, whose correctness is `mergeNode_node`. No
tree grows, so the time is polynomial in the length of the input.

The proof of the main theorem. The algorithm converts the word of the

The Sauer–Shelah lemma. The traces on a set `S` of at most `k` vertices
form a family of subsets of `S` whose shattered sets are shattered by
the neighborhoods of `G`, so they have size at most `d`. By the
Sauer–Shelah lemma of mathlib (via Pajor's bound on the shatterer) the
family has at most `∑_{i ≤ d} C(|S|, i) ≤ (|S| + 1)^d ≤ (k + 1)^d`
members.

As in the paper, every pair `uv ∈ R` has `dist_𝒫(u, v) ≤ 5`. In a
`𝒫`-flip `H`, the bipartite graph `H[X, Y]` is `G[X, Y]` or `Ḡ[X, Y]`,
and the walk of length at most `5` there projects to a walk in `H` by
contracting diagonal edges. A walk of length at most `r` in `R` then
gives a walk of length at most `5r` in every `𝒫`-flip.

The formula of the paper. `θ_S(a, b)` says that `a` and `b` have the
same atomic type over `S`, with one quantifier. `e^±_S(a, b; x, y)` says
that `a` and `b` lie in opposite parts among the parts of `x` and `y`
and are equal or adjacent, respectively non-adjacent. `ρ^±_S(x, y)` says
that there are `z₁, …, z₄` such that every consecutive pair of `x, z₁,
…, z₄, y` satisfies `e^±_S`, and `φ_R = x ≠ y ∧ ρ⁺_S ∧ ρ⁻_S`. Such a
chain is a walk of length `5` between opposite copies of `x` and `y` in
`G[X, Y]`, respectively `Ḡ[X, Y]`. Conversely, every walk of length at
most `5` between opposite copies has odd length and can be padded to
length exactly `5` by going back and forth along an edge. The pair
relation is symmetric, as exchanging the two copies maps `G[X, Y]` to
`G[Y, X]`. The rank is `4 + 1 = 5`.

The paper's formula takes the disjunction over walks of length `1`, `3`
and `5`. The padding argument makes the walks of length `5` suffice.

On two copies of `V`, the graph `G[X, Y]` is a subgraph of `G[X', Y']`
whenever `X ⊆ X'` and `Y ⊆ Y'`, and likewise for `Ḡ[X, Y]`. The parts of
`𝒫` lie in the parts of `𝒫'`, so every short walk witnessing `uv ∈ R(G, 𝒫)`
is a walk in the graphs for `𝒫'`.

Bonnet et al., Lemma 8, for a
partition given by a labeling `V → Fin p`: a refined labeling with at
most `p · 2^p` labels and one toggle on it whose radius-`r` balls lie in
the radius-`6r` balls of the flip metric. Label the parts of `𝒫` by
`Fin |𝒫|`. The fibers of the refined labeling form the partition `𝒬`,
and flips for a labeling with a symmetric toggle are exactly the flips
for its fibers.

The program runs the glue program `ShiftRam.glue` and the restriction
program of the restriction lemma in the loop driver `loop_sound`. In its
first round the glue program reads the tree, finds the first extension
with guard `0`, which exists since `dist(a₁, a₁) = 0`, and asks for the
restriction of its child to the first `ℓ` positions. In its second round
it outputs the answer. The child is `tree_{k+1,q−1}(ā b)` for a vertex
`b`, so the answer is `tree_{k+1,q−1}(ā)`, as in the proof of the rank
shift lemma. Every run inside the driver is right at an admissible word
length: the runs of the glue program because their values are polynomial
in the input, the run of the restriction program because its query is
admissible at the word length of its region. The constant absorbs the
constant of the restriction program at rank `(k + 1, q)`, and the degree
is that of the restriction program plus two.

The program is the loop driver of the glue program of the resolve lift
with the switch of its five callees: the rank shift (the rank shift
lemma), the far tree (the far tree lemma), the far composition (the far
composition lemma), the canonical form (the canonical form observation)
and the scatter type (the lemma on computing scatter types). The glue
program first computes the scatter type of the input, then walks down
the levels of the items, asking for the shift, the far tree and the
compositions of each item, and walks up again, asking for the canonical
forms of the atoms and of the children of each item. Its last round
builds the resolved graph and its distance matrix, by the formula for
distances after a resolve, and writes the output. Every round runs within a constant times `(n + 1)
Y^a` steps, with `Y = M + T + 1`, except the first two and the last
round, which read the input or write the output and run within a
constant times `(n + 1)² Y^a` steps. With at most a constant times `(n +
1)(T + 1)^(q + 1)` rounds, the total time of the glue program is within
the bound. The sizes of the output trees are those of the type trees of
the resolved graph.

The program is one pass over the tree followed by restoring canonical
form, as in the proof of the restriction lemma. The pass reads the tree
and `J`, the latter into a table of the places of the positions, lists
the nodes of the tree in breadth-first order, and writes for every node,
from the last to the first, its transformed atoms and its transformed
extensions. An atom is transformed by renaming its positions along `J`,
and dropped if a position lies outside `J`. An extension is transformed
by renaming its guard in the same way, and dropped if the guard lies
outside `J`, and its child is referred to by the indices of the jobs of
the child. Positions beyond the arity `ℓ`, the new positions of the
nodes below the root, are moved down by `ℓ - |J|`. Nothing is sorted in
the pass. The canonical form is then restored from the leaves up by the
program of the canonical form observation, called once for every set of
the result (`TreeCanon.treeCanon`). The result is the semantic core
`restrictNode` along the partial inverse of `J`, whose correctness is
`restrictTree_tree`. The sets of the result are no larger than those of
the input, so the time is polynomial in the length of the input.

Level `i` of the domain `D_{k+1,q}` is level `i + 1` of `D_{k,q+1}`, since
the ranks and the radius bounds coincide. The values agree because the
caps `(k+1) + q` and `k + (q+1)` coincide and both use the same greedy
scattered set.

Let `h = 7^q` and `r = h + 1`. Expand the colored graph by a relation for
every relation symbol with some positions filled by parameters from `U`,
and by a unary relation `P_u` for every `u ∈ U`. Formulas with parameters
become formulas of the expansion without parameters and with the same
quantifier rank. For a tuple far from `U`, the ball `B` of radius `h` around
it in the expansion avoids `U` and its neighbors, so the new relations are
trivial on `B`, and the type of rank `q'` of the tuple in the expansion of
`B` is determined by its type in the colored graph induced on `B`. By
`LocalToGlobal`, that type determines the type of rank `q` in the expansion,
hence the type over `U` in the colored graph. The types of rank `q'` of
`k`-tuples in colored graphs are bounded by the number of their finite
codes, which depends on `q`, `k` and `c` only.

The bound follows from `SeparatingTypes`, since for a fixed tuple `ū` from
`U` the type of `ā ū` over `U` is determined by the type of `ā` over `U`.
A formula about `ā ū` becomes a formula about `ā` of the same quantifier
rank when the variables for `ū` are replaced by the parameters `ū`.

Let `B` be the radius-`r` ball and `B'` the radius-`(r+1)` ball of the
`𝒬`-flip metric around `v`, and `T' = T ∩ B'`. The transversal has one
vertex in each part of `𝒫`, so `|T'| ≤ |B'/𝒫| ≤ k`. Take `u ∈ B` and
`t ∈ T ∖ B'`. Some `𝒬`-flip `H` has no short walk from `v` to `t`, so
`u` and `t` are distinct and non-adjacent in `H`. Hence the adjacency of
`t` in `G` is the same for all vertices of `B` in the part `𝒬(u)`, which
contains `𝒫(u)`. So the part of `u` in `𝒫 ∧ T` is determined by its part
in `𝒫` and its trace on `T'`. There are at most `k` parts of `𝒫` meeting
`B`, and at most `π_G(k)` traces on `T'`.

As in the paper. If `𝒫ᵢ ≼ 𝒫ⱼ` then a vertex that is minimal in its part
of `𝒫ⱼ` is minimal in its part of `𝒫ᵢ`, so `Tⱼ ⊆ Tᵢ`. Two vertices in
the same part of `𝒬ᵢ` lie in the same part of `𝒫ᵢ`, hence of `𝒫ⱼ`. They
have the same neighbors in `Tᵢ ∖ 𝒫ᵢ(u)`, which contains `Tⱼ ∖ 𝒫ⱼ(u)`, so
they lie in the same part of `𝒬ⱼ`.

The program runs the glue program `FarRam.glue` and the restriction
program of the restriction lemma in the loop driver `loop_sound`. Round
`j` of the glue program reads the tree, the scatter type and the answers
so far, and asks for the restriction `μ ↾ (ℓ+1)` of the child of
extension `j` to its last position, one call per extension. The last
round reads the radius and the blocks off the root, the met and far bits
off the roots of the children, scans the scatter type and writes the
selected trees, as in the proof of the far tree lemma. Its output is the
far tree by `farTree_tree`, which applies the clustering lemma. Every
run inside the driver is right at an admissible word length: the runs of
the glue program because their values are polynomial in the input with a
factor depending on the rank, the runs of the restriction program
because their queries are admissible at the word lengths of their
regions.

The rightwards implication follows from the evaluation lemma: the
evaluation program receives equal inputs for the two tuples, so it gives
equal answers. The vertex type is renamed to `Fin n` for this. The
converse is `node_eq_of_sat_iff`, by induction on `q`.

By induction along the tuple and the triangle inequality, the entry `vᵢ`
is within `∑_{i'=1}^{i} ρ⁺(k+i', q−i')` of `v₀`. A color mentioned in a
true atom of rank `(k+j, q−j)` has a vertex within the radius of the atom,
at most `ρ⁺(k+j, q−j)`, of an entry. The horizon inequality
`guardSum_add_le` bounds both distances by `ρ⁺(k, q)`.

The proof in the paper, with the padding step replaced by a split of
each tuple into its entries outside `U` and its entries inside `U`. Let
`r = r(q)` be the separation radius. For each `k' ≤ k`, the closure
theorem for tuples gives polynomially many `s`-flips `H` of `G` such
that every `k'`-tuple outside `U` is at distance more than `r` from `U`
in one of them. A flip `H` is undone by a toggle on at most `s` parts,
so the edges of `G` are quantifier-free definable in `H` expanded by the
colors and by predicates for the parts, and the type of a tuple in this
expansion `H⁺` determines its type in `G⁺`. A `k`-tuple `v̄` is a
rearrangement of `ā ū` with `ā` outside `U` and `ū` inside `U`, and its
type is determined by the type of `ā ū` and the positions. For fixed
positions, `ū`, and `H`, the tuples `ā` far from `U` in `H` realize at
most `T(q, k', c + s)` types in `H⁺`. Summing over at most `2^k`
position sets, `(|U| + 1)^k` tuples `ū` and the flips gives the bound,
whose exponent does not depend on `c`.

Put `K = |Types_{d,d}(Ball_r(v))|`. By the locality lemma, every node of
`tree_{k,q}(v)` is the tree of a tuple from the ball, and every color in
a true atom of its root meets the ball. There are at most `K` such
colors and at most `K` trees per rank and arity by part (i). So every
root has `O_{k,q}(K)` atoms, every node has at most `(q+1) K` children,
and the depth is `q`. This gives the bound `(3 + D) (K+1)^(q+1)`, where
`D` depends on `k` and `q` only.

A tuple `v̄ ∈ X^ℓ` is padded to a `d`-tuple by repeating its last entry.
The type of quantifier rank `d` of the padded tuple determines the type of
`v̄` of quantifier rank `d`, which determines `tree_{k+i,q−i}(v̄)` by
`tree_eq_of_tp_eq`, since `ρ⁺(k+i, q−i) + q − i ≤ d`. So the type trees
are the image of a function on `Types_{d,d}(X)`.

The finite form of Matoušek's (p, q)-theorem, through ε-nets and the
finite minimax theorem. Its
statement has the roles of the sides swapped and needs no exception for
the vertices of the sample, so it implies the form used here.
